decks.title: Communication at Work
decks.subtitle: Emails, meetings and Slack: who reads what you write?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: use key vocabulary for workplace communication and remote work
read and analyse a text on how offices communicate today
write clear, polite professional emails in the right register
practise exam-style reading and vocabulary tasks

slides.title: Always on?
text: Ten years ago, office communication meant email and the occasional phone call. Today a junior employee in a Lisbon tech company may juggle email, Teams, Slack, WhatsApp groups and video calls before lunch.
Instant messaging has made teams faster, but it has also blurred the line between work and private life. Messages arrive at 10 p.m. and many people feel they must reply at once.

In 2021 Portugal amended its labour law so that employers must, as a rule, avoid contacting staff during their rest time. Critics say a rule on paper changes little if the workplace culture stays the same.
Experts agree on one point: clear writing saves time. A short email with a precise subject line often achieves more than twenty quick chat messages.

slides.title: Reading: true or false?
slides.instruction: Read the text again. Correct the false statements.

items.q: Ten years ago, offices used many messaging apps.
items.fix: Ten years ago, office communication meant mainly email and phone calls.

items.q: Instant messaging has blurred work and private life.
Portugal changed its labour law in 2021.
Critics think the law alone will solve the problem.
items.fix: Critics say a rule on paper changes little if the culture stays the same.

items.q: Experts prefer many short chat messages to one email.
items.fix: A short, precise email often achieves more than twenty chat messages.

left.heading: Email
points: decisions, requests and anything that needs a record
clients, managers, people outside the team
full sentences, greeting and sign-off
one topic per email, clear subject line

right.heading: Chat
points: quick questions and coordination
colleagues you work with every day
short, informal, contractions are fine
never for bad news or sensitive feedback

slides.title: Making your email polite
rows: Could you **send** me the report, please?
**Would it be possible** to arrange a meeting?

**Unfortunately**, I won't be able to attend.
slides.note: Softeners (could, would, I'm afraid, unfortunately) make requests polite without sounding weak.

We **may** need to postpone it. (eventualmente)

decks.title: Global Citizenship
decks.subtitle: Can you belong to one country and to the whole world?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: discuss identity, migration and multicultural societies
use vocabulary to talk about rights, belonging and responsibility
read an opinion text and identify the writer's stance
build arguments for an opinion essay on global citizenship

cards.heading: Awareness
cards.text: Knows that local choices, from clothes to energy, have effects far away.
cards.example: Who **made** my T-shirt, and for how much?

cards.heading: Respect
cards.text: Accepts that other cultures have their own logic, not just 'strange habits'.

cards.heading: Responsibility
cards.text: Acts locally on global problems: volunteering, voting, consuming with care.
cards.example: Helping at a **food bank** in Porto.

slides.title: A country of leavers, now a country of arrivals
text: For most of the twentieth century, Portugal was a country people left. Families from Trás-os-Montes went to Paris, Luxembourg or Toronto, and the August return of the emigrants became part of village life.

The picture has changed. Today Portuguese classrooms include children whose parents came from Brazil, Cape Verde, Nepal, India or Ukraine. In Lisbon's Martim Moniz you can hear dozens of languages in one street.
This raises old questions in a new place. What does it mean to be Portuguese? Is it a passport, a language, a shared history, or simply the decision to live here and contribute?
Perhaps a country that knows how emigration feels is better prepared than most to welcome others.

slides.title: Reading comprehension
slides.instruction: Answer the questions about the text in your own words.

items.q: How was Portugal described in the twentieth century?
items.a: As a country of emigration: many Portuguese left to live abroad.

items.q: What has changed in Portuguese classrooms?
items.a: They now include children of immigrants from many different countries.

items.q: Which question about identity does the writer ask?
items.a: What it means to be Portuguese: a passport, a language, history or contributing.

items.q: What is the writer's attitude in the last paragraph?
items.a: Hopeful: Portugal's emigrant past may help it welcome immigrants.

slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the word in brackets.

Prejudice often comes from ___ of other cultures. (ignore)
Many ___ send money back to their families. (emigrate)
The debate became very ___. (emotion)

left.heading: Benefits
points: cultural exchange: food, music, ideas
student mobility (Erasmus+) and travel
cooperation on climate and health

right.heading: Concerns
points: local traditions and languages disappear

items.en: **It could be argued that** cultural diversity makes societies stronger.
**On the other hand**, rapid change can create tension in communities.
**There is no doubt that** language is the key to integration.
**While** some fear losing their identity, **others** see it as enriched.
**All things considered**, the benefits outweigh the risks.

decks.title: Ethics and Technology
decks.subtitle: Just because we can, does it mean we should?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: talk about AI, data privacy, gene editing and surveillance
read about a real ethical dilemma and evaluate the arguments
use hedging language to express careful opinions
practise exam-style vocabulary and writing tasks

cards.heading: AI at school
cards.text: Help with learning, or a shortcut that hides what students really know?

cards.heading: Your data
cards.text: Free apps are paid for with data. Who owns it and who sells it?

cards.heading: Surveillance
cards.text: Cameras with facial recognition: safer streets or loss of freedom?

cards.heading: Gene editing
cards.text: Curing inherited diseases, or designing 'perfect' babies?

slides.title: The algorithm said no
text: A large company once built a program to sort job applications automatically. It learned from ten years of CVs of people the company had hired, most of whom were men.
The system soon began to give lower scores to CVs that mentioned women's clubs or women's colleges. Nobody had told it to discriminate; it had simply copied the past.
The project was abandoned, but the lesson remains. Algorithms are not neutral just because they are mathematical. They reflect the data they are fed and the choices of the people who design them.
This is why the European Union's AI Act classifies recruitment software as 'high-risk' and demands human oversight.

slides.instruction: Choose the option that is correct according to the text.

slides.text: **Data** is usually treated as uncountable in everyday English. **Information** and **advice** are always uncountable.

decks.title: Democracy and Rights
decks.subtitle: Freedom is not a given. Who keeps it alive?

slides.title: In this lesson you will

practise exam-style tasks on vocabulary and comprehension

slides.title: From 1948 to 1974
text: In December 1948, three years after the end of the Second World War, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its first article states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

In Portugal, however, those words meant little for another 26 years. Under the Estado Novo, newspapers were censored, political parties were banned and opponents were arrested by the political police.

On 25 April 1974, a military coup, soon backed by crowds in the streets, ended the dictatorship almost without bloodshed. A year later, Portuguese citizens voted in the first free elections in decades.
Today the carnation is a reminder that rights written on paper only matter when people defend them.

slides.title: Reading: true or false?
slides.instruction: Decide if the statements are true (T) or false (F). Correct the false ones.

items.q: The Declaration was adopted before the war ended.
items.fix: It was adopted in 1948, three years after the war ended.

items.q: The 1974 revolution was almost bloodless.

decks.title: Global Ethical Issues
decks.subtitle: Who really pays for a five-euro T-shirt?

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: discuss global issues: fast fashion, climate justice, food waste

read and react to a text about the clothing industry

cards.heading: Fast fashion
cards.text: Cheap clothes for us, low wages and unsafe factories for others.

cards.heading: Climate justice
cards.text: The countries that polluted least often suffer the worst heatwaves and floods.

slides.title: The building that fell
text: On 24 April 2013, the Rana Plaza building near Dhaka, Bangladesh, collapsed. It housed several garment factories that produced clothes for well-known Western brands. More than a thousand workers died.
The day before, cracks had appeared in the walls. Workers were told to return anyway; orders had deadlines.
The disaster led to a safety agreement signed by many brands and to the Fashion Revolution movement, which asks consumers a simple question: who made my clothes?

Critics point out that the industry has grown since then, and that cheap clothes are now sold even faster online. Responsibility, they argue, is shared: brands, governments and buyers all have a role.

decks.title: Intercultural Dialogue
decks.subtitle: When 'quite good' means 'not good at all'

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: understand direct and indirect communication styles

left.heading: More direct
points: say 'no' clearly; frankness shows respect
criticism is specific and open
the message is in the words
often linked to Germany, the Netherlands

right.heading: More indirect
points: avoid open conflict; 'no' is softened
criticism is hidden in praise
the message is in context and tone
often linked to Japan, and to the UK

slides.title: Generalisations, not rules
slides.text: These are **tendencies**, not facts about every person. Use them to understand, never to judge or label individuals.

slides.note: Tone matters too: 'quite good' said with enthusiasm can be positive. Context decides.

slides.title: The Portuguese stereotype
text: Ask a foreign student in Lisbon to describe the Portuguese and you may hear: friendly, but late; humble, maybe too humble; quick to complain about their own country, quick to defend it against outsiders.
Stereotypes contain a grain of truth and a lot of simplification. A dinner at nine with grandparents in Viseu is not the same as a startup meeting in Porto.
Intercultural competence is not memorising lists of habits. It means noticing your own assumptions, asking before judging and adapting without losing yourself.

Soften with **I'm afraid**, **would you mind**, **I'm not sure**.
Intercultural competence: **notice**, **ask**, **adapt**.

slides.title: Reading Austen's first line
text: The opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice (1813) sounds like a serious general law. Read it twice, though, and the irony appears.
It is not the rich young man who desperately wants a wife. It is the families around him, with daughters and very little money, who have decided that he must want one.
In a society where women could rarely earn their own income, marriage was an economic question. Austen makes us smile, and then makes us think.
This mix of humour and social criticism is one reason why her novels are still adapted for film and TV more than two centuries later.

slides.title: Reading: true or false?
slides.instruction: Decide if the statements are true (T) or false (F). Correct the false ones.

items.q: Pride and Prejudice was published in 1813.
The first line should be read literally.
items.fix: The first line is ironic.

items.q: The rich man is desperate to get married.
items.fix: The families around him have decided that he wants a wife.

items.q: For women, marriage was also about money.
Austen combines humour with social criticism.

slides.instruction: Answer in two or three sentences about a book you have read.

items.a: It is set in a small town and follows a girl who investigates her brother's disappearance.

slides.title: Discuss
questions: Why do we still read Shakespeare 400 years later?
Is it better to read a classic or watch the film?
Which two roads have you had to choose between?
Should schools teach more contemporary authors?
Do you read more in Portuguese or in English?

slides.title: Remember
points: Key terms: **plot**, **setting**, **narrator**, **theme**, **irony**.
**Novel** (romance) is not the same as 'novela' (soap opera).
Classics: Shakespeare, Austen, Dickens, Wilde, Twain, Frost.
Modern voices: Orwell, Morrison, Ishiguro, Adichie.

decks.title: Verb Tenses Review
decks.subtitle: Twelve tenses, one exam: choose the right one every time

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: review present, past and future tenses in simple, continuous and perfect forms
identify time expressions that signal each tense
avoid the classic errors Portuguese speakers make
solve exam-style gap-fill and error-correction tasks

slides.title: Talking about the future
rows: in progress at a future time
slides.note: After when, as soon as, until, before, after: present tense, not will. 'When I **finish**', never 'when I will finish'.

slides.title: Choose the right tense
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: I ___ here since September.
By the time we arrived, the match ___.
Call me as soon as you ___ the results.
This time tomorrow I ___ the exam.
She ___ when the lights went out.
Why are you so tired? I ___ for hours.

slides.title: Classic Portuguese errors
slides.text: Portuguese uses the present for duration ('Vivo cá há 3 anos'). English needs the **present perfect**. And no present perfect with finished time.
examples: I **have lived** here for 3 years. (not 'I live here for')
I **saw** him yesterday. (not 'I have seen him yesterday')
How long **have you known** her? (not 'do you know')

cards.heading: Mind
cards.text: know, believe, understand, remember: no continuous form.

cards.heading: Feelings
cards.text: like, love, hate, prefer, want, need.

cards.heading: Two meanings
cards.text: think, have, see, taste: action meaning allows -ing.
cards.example: I'**m thinking** about it. / I **think** so.

slides.title: Exam practice: complete the text
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.

items.q: Ana ___ (study) in Porto for two years now.
Before she moved, she ___ (never / live) alone.
Last summer she ___ (work) in a café in Lagos.
While she ___ (serve) tables, she met Tom.
By 2030 she ___ (finish) her medical degree.
She ___ (fly) to London next Friday; it's booked.

slides.title: Find and correct the error
slides.instruction: Each sentence has one tense error. Rewrite it correctly.

items.q: I know him since primary school.
items.a: I have known him since primary school.

items.q: We have visited London in 2022.
I'll text you when I will arrive.
items.a: I'll text you when I arrive.

items.q: She is having two brothers.
When I got home, my parents already left.
items.a: When I got home, my parents had already left.

slides.title: Time expressions
slides.instruction: Match each time expression to the tense it usually goes with.

items.q: yesterday, in 2019, ago
already, yet, ever, so far
by the time, before that
by next year, by then
at the moment, these days

slides.title: Remember
points: Duration up to now: **present perfect (continuous)**, not present simple.
Finished time (yesterday, in 2022): **past simple**.
After **when / as soon as**: present tense for the future.
Stative verbs (know, want, belong) avoid the **-ing** form.
Earlier past: **had + past participle**.

decks.title: Inversion
decks.subtitle: Never have I seen a sentence start like this

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: understand why and when English inverts subject and verb
use negative adverbials: never, rarely, not only, no sooner
form inverted conditionals: had I known, should you need
transform sentences in exam-style rewriting tasks

cards.heading: Like a question
cards.text: The auxiliary comes before the subject, but the sentence is a statement.
cards.example: **Never have I** seen such a crowd.

cards.heading: Why use it?
cards.text: Emphasis and drama. It is typical of formal writing, speeches and news.

cards.heading: No auxiliary?
cards.text: Add **do / does / did**, as in questions.

slides.title: Negative and limiting adverbials
rows: **Seldom have we** had such a good team.
**Not only did he** lie, but he also stole.
**No sooner had I** sat down than the phone rang.
**Hardly had we** arrived when it began to rain.
**Under no circumstances should you** open it.
**Little did they** know what was coming.
slides.note: With Only when / Only after / Not until, the inversion happens in the second (main) clause.

slides.title: Watch out!
slides.text: **No sooner** goes with **than**; **hardly** and **scarcely** go with **when**. Both usually take the past perfect.
examples: No sooner had he left **than** she called. (not 'when')
Hardly had the film started **when** the power went off.

slides.title: Choose the correct form
slides.instruction: Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

items.q: Never ___ such a beautiful sunset.
Rarely ___ late for school.
Not only ___ the exam, but she got top marks.
No sooner had we left ___ it started to snow.
Little ___ that they were being filmed.

slides.title: Inverted conditionals (formal)
rows: If you need help, call me.
If I were rich, I'd travel.
If I had known, I'd have come.
slides.note: Drop 'if' and invert. The negative is not contracted: 'Had they not', never 'Hadn't they'.

slides.title: Rewrite with inversion
slides.instruction: Rewrite each sentence starting with the words given.

items.q: I have never felt so nervous. (Never...)
items.a: Never have I felt so nervous.

items.q: You must not use your phone in the exam. (Under no circumstances...)
items.a: Under no circumstances must you use your phone in the exam.

items.q: If I had known about the strike, I'd have walked. (Had...)
items.a: Had I known about the strike, I'd have walked.

items.q: If you have any questions, please email us. (Should...)
items.a: Should you have any questions, please email us.

items.q: I only understood the joke when I got home. (Only when...)
items.a: Only when I got home did I understand the joke.

slides.title: Complete the inversions
slides.instruction: Complete with the verbs in brackets, using inversion.

items.q: Seldom ___ such a talented player. (we / see)
Not only ___ late, but he also forgot his ID. (he / be)
Hardly ___ when the fire alarm rang. (the test / start)
___ rich, I would buy a flat in Lisbon. (I / be)
Only after the match ___ the truth. (they / learn)

items.en: **Not until** the final whistle **did** the fans start to celebrate.
**Should** you require assistance, please contact reception.
**At no time were** the passengers in danger.
**So tired was she** that she fell asleep on the bus.
**Only then did** we realise how serious it was.

slides.title: Exam practice: key word transformation
slides.instruction: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first.

items.q: He never apologised. At no time ___.
If they call, say I am out. Should ___, say I am out.
I had just sat down when the bell rang. No sooner ___ the bell rang.
She was so talented that she won a prize. So ___ that she won a prize.
I didn't know it was a trap. Little ___ it was a trap.

slides.title: Remember
points: Negative adverbial at the start: **auxiliary + subject**.
No auxiliary? Use **do / does / did**: Rarely **does** she...
**No sooner... than**; **hardly / scarcely... when**.
Formal conditionals: **Should you**, **Were I**, **Had I known**.
Inversion is formal: great for essays, odd in casual chat.

decks.title: Cleft Sentences
decks.subtitle: What really matters is where you put the focus

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: use it-clefts to focus on a person, thing, time or place
use what-clefts to highlight an idea or an action
use all, the thing, the reason, the place in cleft structures
transform sentences for emphasis, as in the national exam

left.heading: Neutral
points: Rita broke the window.
I need a long holiday.
The noise annoys me.
We met in Coimbra.

right.heading: Cleft (emphatic)
points: **It was Rita who** broke the window.
**What I need is** a long holiday.
**What annoys me is** the noise.
**It was in Coimbra that** we met.

slides.title: It-clefts
rows: **It was my gran who** taught me.
**It's in Porto that** I feel home.
**It was because of** the rain **that** we left.
slides.note: Use 'It is' for present focus and 'It was' for past events. The verb after who/that agrees with X.

slides.title: It-clefts
slides.instruction: Rewrite each sentence with It is / It was, focusing on the words in bold.

items.q: **Carlos** scored the winning goal.
items.a: It was Carlos who scored the winning goal.

items.q: We moved to the Algarve **in 2020**.
items.a: It was in 2020 that we moved to the Algarve.

items.q: I'm worried about **the exam**, not the results.
items.a: It's the exam that I'm worried about, not the results.

items.q: My sister lent me **this jacket**.
items.a: It was this jacket that my sister lent me.

slides.title: What-clefts and similar
rows: **What I love about summer is** the light.
**What he did was (to) call** the police.
**What happened was that** the bus broke down.
**All I want is** a good night's sleep.
**The reason why I left is that** I was bored.
slides.note: 'All I want' means 'the only thing I want'. 'The reason why... is that', not 'is because' in formal English.

slides.title: Watch out!
slides.text: Never put **it** after **what** in these structures, and keep the right verb form after 'do'.
examples: **What I need is** sleep. (not 'What I need it is')
What she **did was apply** again. (not 'was applied')
**All you need is** patience.

slides.title: What-clefts
slides.instruction: Complete the sentences so they mean the same as the first one.

items.q: I really need a break. What ___ a break.
Her attitude surprised me. What ___ her attitude.
He just shrugged. All ___ shrug.
I want to travel. What ___ to travel.
The train was cancelled. What ___ that the train was cancelled.

slides.title: Spot the correct sentence
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: Choose the correct cleft.
options: What I hate it is waiting.

items.q: Choose the correct cleft.
options: It was my parents who paid.
It were my parents who paid.
items.a: It was my parents who paid.

items.q: Choose the correct cleft.
options: What we did was call a taxi.
What we did was called a taxi.
items.a: What we did was call a taxi.

items.q: Choose the formal option.
options: The reason is that it's late.
The reason is because it's late.
items.a: The reason is that it's late.

items.en: **What worries scientists most is** the speed of the change.
**It is young people who** will live with these decisions.
**All we ask is** to be heard.
**The place where** I feel most relaxed **is** my grandparents' village.
**It wasn't until** I moved abroad **that** I valued Portuguese food.

slides.title: Exam practice: emphasise it
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences beginning with the words given.

items.q: I only realised how lucky I was later. (It wasn't until...)
items.a: It wasn't until later that I realised how lucky I was.

items.q: She only wanted some respect. (All...)
items.a: All she wanted was some respect.

items.q: I left because the music was too loud. (The reason...)
items.a: The reason why I left was that the music was too loud.

items.q: The ending of the film disappointed me. (What...)
items.a: What disappointed me was the ending of the film.

slides.title: Remember
points: **It is/was + X + who/that** focuses on one element.
**What + clause + is/was** highlights an idea or action.
**All I want is...** = the only thing I want.
**It wasn't until... that** stresses a late moment.
Formal: **the reason is that**, not 'because'.

decks.title: Participle Clauses
decks.subtitle: Having learnt this, you'll write shorter, smarter sentences

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: use present, past and perfect participle clauses
express time, reason, result and condition more concisely
reduce relative clauses with -ing and -ed forms
avoid dangling participles, a common exam error

slides.title: Three types of participle
rows: **Built** in 1886, the bridge links Porto and Gaia.
**Having finished** my essay, I went out.
slides.note: Present participles are active; past participles are usually passive in meaning.

cards.heading: Time
cards.text: When, while, after...
cards.example: **Arriving** at the station, I called mum.

cards.heading: Reason
cards.text: Because, as, since...

cards.heading: Result
cards.text: So, and as a result...
cards.example: It rained all day, **ruining** the festival.

cards.heading: Condition
cards.text: If...

slides.title: Combine the sentences
slides.instruction: Rewrite as one sentence using a participle clause.

items.q: She opened the letter. She started to cry.
items.a: Opening the letter, she started to cry.

items.q: Because I didn't know the way, I used my phone.
items.a: Not knowing the way, I used my phone.

items.q: After he had saved enough money, he bought a car.
items.a: Having saved enough money, he bought a car.

items.q: The book was written in 1847. It is still popular.
items.a: Written in 1847, the book is still popular.

slides.title: Watch out! Dangling participles
slides.text: The participle clause and the main clause must have the **same subject**. Otherwise the result is wrong and often funny.
examples: Walking to school, **the rain** started. (the rain walking?)
Walking to school, **I** got caught in the rain.
**Having** eaten, the plates were washed. (wrong)
Having eaten, **we** washed the plates. (right)

slides.title: Correct or dangling?
slides.instruction: Decide if each sentence is correct (T) or has a dangling participle (F).

items.q: Looking out of the window, I saw a fox.
Running for the bus, my phone fell out.
items.fix: Running for the bus, I dropped my phone.

items.q: Having read the reviews, we booked the hotel.
Covered in mud, mum made me shower.
items.fix: Covered in mud, I had to shower.

items.q: Exhausted after the match, the players slept.

items.en: The woman **who is sitting** by the door = the woman **sitting** by the door.
Products **that are made** in Portugal = products **made** in Portugal.
Anyone **who wishes** to apply = anyone **wishing** to apply.
The documents **that were sent** yesterday = the documents **sent** yesterday.

slides.title: Present or past participle?
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct participle of the verb in brackets.

items.q: Students ___ (want) to join should sign up today.
The azulejos ___ (use) in the station are original.
___ (finish) her shift, the nurse drove home.
The boy ___ (stand) next to Rui is my cousin.
___ (not / invite), we stayed at home.
items.a: Not having been invited / Not invited

items.q: A storm hit the coast, ___ (leave) thousands without power.

slides.title: Exam practice: formal writing
slides.instruction: Choose the option that best completes each sentence.

items.q: ___ by millions, the app collects huge amounts of data.
___ the instructions, he couldn't assemble the desk.
Prices rose sharply, ___ many families in difficulty.
___ in Lisbon, Pessoa wrote under many names.

slides.title: Remember
points: **-ing** = active; **past participle** = passive meaning.
**Having + past participle** shows the first of two actions.
Negative: put **not** before the participle.
Same subject in both clauses: avoid **dangling** participles.
Reduce relative clauses: the man **sitting** there.

decks.title: Advanced Conditionals
decks.subtitle: If I had studied harder, I would be calmer now

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: review the four basic conditional types quickly
form mixed conditionals linking past and present
use unless, provided that, as long as, otherwise, but for
transform conditional sentences in exam-style tasks

slides.title: Quick review
rows: If it rains, we'**ll stay** in.
If we'**d left**, we'**d have made** it.
slides.note: Could, might and should can replace will or would: If you asked her, she **might** say yes.

left.heading: Past cause, present result
points: If + past perfect, would + verb
If I **had taken** the job, I **would live** in Paris now.
If she **hadn't missed** the train, she'**d be** here.
Often with now, today, still

right.heading: Present cause, past result
points: If + past simple, would have + p.p.
If I **were** braver, I'**d have spoken** up.
If he **spoke** English, he'**d have got** the job.
The condition is a permanent truth

slides.title: Mixed conditionals
slides.instruction: Complete with the correct form of the verbs in brackets.

items.q: If I ___ (go) to bed earlier, I wouldn't be so tired now.
If she weren't so shy, she ___ (ask) him out last week.
If we had bought that flat, we ___ (be) rich today.
If he ___ (not / be) so stubborn, he'd have listened.
If they ___ (invest) in 2010, they'd own the company now.

slides.title: Alternatives to 'if'
rows: **Provided that** you pay, you can go.
**As long as** you're back by 11, fine.
**Supposing** you won, what would you do?
if it weren't / hadn't been for
**But for** the goalkeeper, we'd have lost.
Take a coat **in case** it rains.
slides.note: 'In case' is not 'if': it means doing something now to be ready for a possible event.

slides.title: Watch out!
slides.text: **Unless** already contains the negative. Do not add another 'not'. And never use **will** in the condition clause.
examples: **Unless** you study, you'll fail. (not 'unless you don't study')
**If** it **rains** tomorrow... (not 'if it will rain')
**I wish** I **had known**. = If only I had known.

slides.title: Choose the best linker
slides.instruction: Choose the option that correctly completes each sentence.

items.q: You can borrow my car ___ you drive carefully.
Take some money ___ you need a taxi.
We'll go to the beach ___ it rains.
___ your help, I'd never have finished.
Write it down, ___ you'll forget.

items.en: **Had** Portugal **invested** earlier in rail, the Lisbon-Porto trip **would be** faster today.
**Provided that** emissions fall, the worst effects **can** still be avoided.
**But for** the lifeguard, the tourist **would have drowned**.
**Supposing** you **could** vote at 16, **would** you?
**If** it **weren't for** my grandmother, I **wouldn't speak** French.

slides.title: Exam practice: rewrite
slides.instruction: Rewrite each sentence using the word in brackets. Keep the meaning.

items.q: If you don't apologise, she won't forgive you. (unless)
items.a: Unless you apologise, she won't forgive you.

items.q: I didn't study, so I'm worried now. (if)
items.a: If I had studied, I wouldn't be worried now.

items.q: Without the GPS, we would have got lost. (but for)
items.a: But for the GPS, we would have got lost.

items.q: You can come only if you bring food. (provided)
items.a: You can come provided (that) you bring food.

items.q: If I had known, I would have told you. (Had)
items.a: Had I known, I would have told you.

slides.title: What if...?
questions: If you had been born in 1950, how would your life be different?
Supposing you could change one decision, what would it be?
Where would you live now if you could choose?
What would happen if social media disappeared tomorrow?

slides.title: Remember
points: Past cause, present result: **If I had... , I would...**
Present cause, past result: **If I were..., I would have...**
**Unless** = if not; **provided / as long as** = only if.
**In case** = as a precaution; **but for** = without.
No **will** after if, unless, provided, in case.

decks.title: Reported Speech & Passive
decks.subtitle: It is said that this is the most tested grammar in the exam

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: report statements, questions and requests accurately
use reporting verbs: suggest, deny, admit, warn, refuse
form the passive in all tenses and with modals
use impersonal passives: it is said that, he is thought to

slides.title: Reported speech: backshift
rows: there, that day, the next day
slides.note: No backshift is needed if the fact is still true: She said she lives in Faro (she still does).

cards.heading: Yes/No questions
cards.text: Use if / whether and normal word order.

cards.heading: Wh- questions
cards.text: Keep the wh- word, no do/did, no inversion.

cards.heading: Commands
cards.text: tell / ask + object + (not) to + verb.

slides.title: Report it
slides.instruction: Rewrite in reported speech.

items.q: 'Where did you buy those trainers?' Rui asked me.
items.a: Rui asked me where I had bought those trainers.

items.q: 'Are you coming tonight?' she asked.
items.a: She asked if / whether I was coming that night.

items.q: 'Don't touch the screen,' the teacher told us.
items.a: The teacher told us not to touch the screen.

items.q: 'I'll send it tomorrow,' he said.
items.a: He said (that) he would send it the next / following day.

slides.title: Reporting verbs
slides.note: Suggest: 'He suggested going' or 'He suggested that we (should) go'. Never 'suggested us to go'.

slides.title: Reporting verbs
slides.instruction: Report each sentence using the verb in brackets.

items.q: 'I didn't take your charger!' He ___ my charger. (deny)
'Let's order pizza.' She ___ pizza. (suggest)
'I'll help you move.' Tiago ___ me move. (offer)
'You cheated!' They ___ cheating. (accuse)
'Don't forget your passport.' Mum ___ my passport. (remind)

slides.title: The passive in all tenses
rows: has been made / had been made
will be made / must be made
slides.note: Use 'by' only when the agent is important or new information.

items.en: People say that the minister will resign. = **It is said that** the minister will resign.
= The minister **is said to be** about to resign.
Experts believe the fire started at night. = The fire **is believed to have started** at night.
They think he lives abroad. = He **is thought to live** abroad.
Causative: I **had my phone repaired**. We **got the house painted**.

slides.title: Exam practice: passive transformations
slides.instruction: Rewrite the sentences in the passive, beginning with the words given.

items.q: They are building a new hospital in Seixal. (A new hospital...)
items.a: A new hospital is being built in Seixal.

items.q: Someone should have told us. (We...)
People believe that the painting is fake. (The painting...)
items.a: The painting is believed to be fake.

items.q: They say the band split up in 2019. (The band...)
items.a: The band is said to have split up in 2019.

items.q: A mechanic is fixing my bike. (I'm having...)

slides.title: Remember
points: Backshift tenses and time words; questions use **statement order**.
Commands: **tell / ask + object + (not) to**.
**Deny / admit / suggest + -ing**; **refuse / offer + to**.
Passive = **be** (in any tense) **+ past participle**.
**It is said that... / He is said to (have)...**

decks.title: Modal Verbs Review
decks.subtitle: You must have heard of them. You needn't have worried.

slides.title: In this lesson you will
items: review modals of ability, permission, obligation and advice
express deduction about the present and the past
distinguish needn't have, didn't need to and shouldn't have
choose the most precise modal in exam tasks

slides.title: Functions at a glance
slides.note: Must = obligation from the speaker; have to = external rule. Mustn't (proibido) is not don't have to (não é preciso).

slides.title: Choose the right modal
slides.instruction: Choose the correct option.

items.q: You ___ wear a uniform; it's optional.
You ___ smoke here. It's a hospital.
After hours of trying, I ___ open the jar.
When I was ten, I ___ swim really well.
We ___ leave early yesterday because of the strike.

slides.title: Could or managed to?
slides.text: For general past ability use **could**. For one specific success use **managed to** or **was able to**. In the negative, **couldn't** works for both.
examples: She **could** read at four. (general)
The firefighters **managed to** rescue the dog. (specific)
I **couldn't** find my keys this morning.

slides.title: Deduction: how sure are you?
slides.note: The opposite of 'must be' for deduction is 'can't be', never 'mustn't be'.

slides.title: Make deductions
slides.instruction: Complete with must, might or can't + the correct form of the verb.

items.q: Her lights are off. She ___ (be) asleep.
He ___ (see) me; he was looking the other way.
The roads are wet. It ___ (rain) last night.
I'm not sure where Ana is. She ___ (be) at the gym.
That ___ (be) Joana. She's in London this week.
Her phone is dead. She ___ (forget) to charge it, perhaps.

slides.title: Needn't have or didn't need to?

left.heading: needn't have + p.p.
points: You did it, but it wasn't necessary.
I **needn't have bought** milk; we had some.
Feeling: wasted effort

right.heading: didn't need to + verb
points: It wasn't necessary (usually not done).
I **didn't need to** buy milk, so I didn't.

story.title: Reading Backwards
story.subtitle: A year in Porto and a secret fifty years old
story.blurb: Inês Carvalho only wanted a Saturday job. Instead, a typed advertisement on Rua das Flores leads her to a locked cabinet, a box of forbidden translations and a mark she has known all her life. Two old letters, written half a century apart, accuse two different men of the same betrayal. One of them is her grandfather.

characters.name: Inês Carvalho
characters.desc: is seventeen and in her final year at a secondary school in Porto. She is better at writing formal letters than at saying what she feels.

characters.name: Joaquim Carvalho
characters.desc: is Inês's grandfather, a retired typographer who still sits facing the door in every café and never talks about the years before the revolution.

characters.name: Margaret Hale
characters.desc: runs Hale Translations. Born in Porto into a British port wine family, she is precise, sharp-tongued and loyal to a father who died believing he had been betrayed.

characters.name: Tomás Reis
characters.desc: is Inês's oldest friend, a gifted programmer who believes that most problems have a technical solution.

characters.name: Daniel Okafor
characters.desc: is the agency's project manager, a Londoner with Nigerian parents who speaks four languages and listens carefully in all of them.

characters.name: Edward Hale
characters.desc: was Margaret's father, a wine merchant who loved Dickens and Porto and left Portugal in 1973 without saying goodbye.

chapters.title: Dear Sir or Madam
paragraphs: The advertisement had been taped to the inside of a café window on Rua das Flores, next to a poster for a fado night. Inês Carvalho noticed it for two reasons: it was written in English, and somebody had typed it on a real typewriter. Every "e" was fainter than the other letters, as if that key had been pressed too often for too many years.

HALE TRANSLATIONS. Junior Assistant required, Saturdays, 9.00 to 14.00. Excellent written English essential. Applicants should send a cover letter and CV to the address below. Only candidates who follow these instructions will be considered.
"'Only candidates who follow these instructions,'" Tomás read over her shoulder, a custard tart in one hand. "That's not an advert. That's a threat."
"It's a test," said Inês.
"Everything is a test for you. You'll probably revise for your own funeral."

She ignored him and took a photo. It was the first week of her final year at school. In nine months she would sit her national exams, and in a year, if everything went according to plan, she would be studying law in Lisbon or languages in Coimbra. What had already been decided was that she needed money, experience that looked good on paper, and an excuse to leave the flat on Saturday mornings, when her mother was sleeping after a night shift at the hospital and her grandfather was listening to the radio loud enough for the whole building.

She wrote the letter that evening at the kitchen table. Her first draft began "Hi! I saw your ad and I really think I'd be perfect for it", and she deleted it before Tomás could see it. The second draft was so stiff that it sounded like a will. On Monday she showed the third one to Professora Matos, who read it in silence.

"Better," said Professora Matos, which from her was almost a hug. "But nobody applies for 'the job of the advertisement'. You apply for a position which was advertised. And you cannot write 'I am very hardworker'. You are hard-working, or you are a hard worker. Choose one."
"Should I say that I've never worked in an office?"

"You mustn't lie. But you needn't confess either. You have been tutoring younger students for two years, haven't you? That is experience. Put it in, and let them decide what it is worth. And if you don't know the name, it is 'Dear Sir or Madam' and 'Yours faithfully'. Never 'Hello'."
The version Inês finally sent on Thursday was short, and she read it so often that the words stopped meaning anything.

Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to apply for the position of Junior Assistant, which was advertised on Rua das Flores. I am currently in my final year of secondary school, and I have been tutoring students in English for the past two years. Although I have not worked in a professional office before, I am organised and reliable, and I am used to meeting deadlines. Furthermore, as chair of my school's debate club, I have learnt to listen carefully and to express ideas clearly under pressure. I look forward to hearing from you. Yours faithfully, Inês Carvalho.
The reply arrived on Tuesday, and she read it in the school canteen with Tomás's elbow in her ribs.

"'Ms Carvalho,'" he read aloud, after stealing her phone. "'Please come for an interview on Saturday at 10.00. Do not be late. M. Hale.' No 'kind regards', no 'best wishes'. This woman is going to eat you alive."

The building was one of those tall, thin houses in the old part of the city that seem to be held up by their neighbours. The wooden stairs complained at every step, and the air smelt of paper and coffee. On the third floor a small brass plate said HALE TRANSLATIONS, ESTABLISHED 1981. It had been polished so often that the letters had gone soft at the edges.
The door was opened by a tall young man with his sleeves rolled up and a pencil behind his ear.

"You must be Inês. You're early." He smiled. "She can't stand people who are late. She can't stand people who are early either, but she hates them less. I'm Daniel Okafor. I manage the projects, which means I tell translators they're brilliant and then tell clients the translators are nearly finished."
His English was London English, quick and full of swallowed consonants, but when Inês answered in Portuguese out of pure nerves, he switched languages without a pause.

Margaret Hale was waiting in an office at the back, behind a desk that had disappeared under dictionaries. She was in her sixties, small and straight-backed, with white hair cut very short and reading glasses on a chain around her neck. On a table by the wall stood something under a grey cloth cover, about the size of a large shoebox.

"Sit down, Ms Carvalho. I have read your CV. It says you are reliable and hard-working. Everybody's CV says that. It is like saying that you have a nose. Tell me something about yourself that isn't true of everyone."
Inês had prepared answers to a dozen questions. This was not one of them. She heard herself say: "I learnt to read from metal letters. Upside down and backwards."
One of Margaret Hale's eyebrows rose by about a millimetre.

"My grandfather had a printing workshop. The old kind, where you set every letter by hand. When I was small he used to let me make my name in the composing stick. The letters are reversed, so you read them like a mirror. I could read my name backwards before I could read it the right way round." She stopped. "That probably isn't useful for translation."

"On the contrary. Translation is mostly reading things backwards." Ms Hale slid a sheet of paper across the desk. "A client received this from a supplier in Manchester. Translate it into Portuguese for the client's director. You have fifteen minutes."

It was an email, and it was furious. Your lot have completely messed up the brochure. We asked for the blue logo and you've gone and put the green one on five thousand copies. Sort it out by Friday or we're done. Inês read it twice, took a breath and wrote. Margaret Hale read her version in silence, tapping the page with her pen.
"'Your lot'. You have translated it as 'a vossa empresa'. Why?"

"Because the original is rude, but the director doesn't need the rudeness. He needs the information. If I'd translated every word, he might have thought the supplier was insulting him personally. The supplier is angry, but he isn't insulting anybody. He's just from Manchester."
Daniel, who was standing in the doorway, made a sound that might have been a laugh.

"You could have kept a little more of the anger," said Ms Hale. "'Or we're done' is a threat, and you have made it sound like a suggestion. Clients should know when they are being threatened. However, you have understood the main thing, which most people never do: a translation is not a copy. It is a decision." She put the paper down. "We pay seven euros an hour. You will answer the phone, check documents, make coffee for Daniel, and you will not talk about our clients to anyone. One more question." She took off her glasses and let them drop on their chain. "Your grandfather. The one with the metal letters. What is his name?"
"Joaquim. Joaquim Carvalho. His workshop was in Miragaia, near the river, but he closed it years ago."
Something happened to the room. Margaret Hale sat very still, and Daniel's smile slowly left his face.
"I see," said Ms Hale. She picked up the CV, folded it in half and then in half again. "In that case, Ms Carvalho, I'm afraid I cannot offer you the position."
"I don't understand. Was my translation..."
"Your translation was excellent. This has nothing to do with your translation." Her voice was perfectly polite and perfectly cold. "Daniel will show you out."

On the landing, Daniel searched his pockets for the key to the street door and did not look at her. "I've worked for her for four years," he said quietly. "She's sacked clients. She's sacked translators. Once she sacked a printer for using the wrong font. But I've never seen her do that."

He started down the stairs. Inês was about to follow him when she heard it through the half-open office door: Margaret Hale's voice, speaking Portuguese, very low, the way people talk to someone who is no longer alive.
"Cinquenta anos. Fifty years, and it's his granddaughter who knocks on my door."

chapters.title: The Locked Cabinet
paragraphs: Her grandfather was in the kitchen when she got home, peeling potatoes over an old copy of the Jornal de Notícias, the way he had done every Saturday of her life. The radio was on. A man was shouting about a penalty.
"I had an interview," Inês said. "At a translation agency. Hale Translations, on Rua das Flores."
The knife stopped.
"Hale," her grandfather repeated. He did not turn round.
"Margaret Hale. She's English, but she was born here. Do you know her?"
"I knew a Hale once. A long time ago." He put the knife down very carefully on the newspaper, as if it might break. "Stay away from that office, Inês."
"Why? What happened?"
"Because I'm asking you to." He switched off the radio, which he never did during a match, and went to his room. The door closed without a sound.

Her mother came out of the bedroom an hour later with her hair in a towel and listened to the whole story while she made coffee. "Don't take it personally," she said. "Your grandfather has never told me anything about his life before the revolution. Nothing. When I was your age I asked him how he'd got the scar on his wrist, and he said he'd fallen off a bicycle." She looked at the closed door. "He has never owned a bicycle."
On Sunday night, an email arrived.

Dear Ms Carvalho, I owe you an apology. My decision yesterday was hasty and unprofessional, and it was not based on your abilities, which are considerable. If you are still interested, I would like to offer you the position on a trial basis, starting next Saturday. I would be grateful if you could confirm by Wednesday. Yours sincerely, Margaret Hale.
She forwarded it to Tomás, who replied in under ten seconds: "omg TAKE IT. but also she is clearly a villain. take it anyway."

Inês spent two days not deciding. She should have told her grandfather. She knew that. But every time she imagined the conversation, it ended with the door closing without a sound again, so on Wednesday morning she wrote her reply on the bus, deleted "Hi Margaret" three times and finally sent: Dear Ms Hale, Thank you for your email. I am pleased to accept the position and will be at the office on Saturday at 9.00. Kind regards, Inês Carvalho. At dinner she told her family that she had found a Saturday job in an office in the Baixa. It was not a lie. It was simply not the whole truth, and she was surprised how easy it was to say.

By the end of October she had learnt more about professional communication than in five years of English lessons. She had learnt to answer the phone with "Hale Translations, good morning, how may I help you?" without sounding like a robot. She had learnt that you never write "You forgot to send the documents" to a client; you write "It seems that we have not yet received the documents". She had learnt that "Cheers" is acceptable at the end of an email to a translator in Bristol and a disaster at the end of an email to a law firm in Lisbon, because she had made exactly that mistake in her second week.
"Don't worry," Daniel had said. "My first week here I wrote 'Love, Daniel' to a notary. Margaret made me write him a formal letter of apology. By hand."

Margaret Hale treated Inês with an exact, careful politeness, the way you might treat a dog that has bitten someone you know. She corrected her work in green ink. She never raised her voice. Once, when Inês had been working there for three weeks, she asked, without looking up from her desk, "Does your grandfather still print?" and when Inês said that his hands shook too much now, Margaret Hale was silent for so long that Inês thought she had not heard.

There were rules, and Margaret explained them on the first day as if she were reading a contract. Clients' names were never mentioned outside the office. Confidential documents, such as medical reports, contracts and asylum papers, were never pasted into online translation tools. "When you put a text into one of those machines," she said, "you don't know where it goes, who reads it, or what it is used for afterwards. Our clients trust us with their lives. Sometimes literally."
Tomás thought this was hilarious. "She's a dinosaur. I translate everything with AI. My last essay for Philosophy was half written by a chatbot and I got a seventeen."
"Then you should have got an eight and a half."

The last rule was not spoken. In the narrow back room, between the photocopier and the window, stood a grey metal cabinet with four drawers and a lock. Margaret Hale kept the key on the same chain as her reading glasses.

"Don't ask," Daniel said, when he saw Inês looking at it. "I asked once, in my first month. The next morning she gave me three hundred pages of fishing regulations to proofread. In Portuguese. About cod."

On the last Saturday of October, Margaret left at eleven to catch a train to Lisbon, where she was interpreting at a conference on Monday. Daniel left at twelve for a meeting with a client in Matosinhos. "Lock up when you go," he said, throwing her the spare key. "And if the phone rings, you're the whole company."

The phone did not ring. The office went quiet in that particular way old buildings go quiet, with small noises in the walls. Inês finished checking a contract, filed three invoices in the back room and was turning to leave when she noticed that the top drawer of the grey cabinet was not completely closed. Margaret must have taken something out before leaving for the train and forgotten to turn the key. It was ajar by perhaps a centimetre.
She stood there for a long moment. She could have closed it. She should have closed it. Later she would tell herself that she had meant to close it, and that her hand had simply slipped. It had not.
Inside there was only one thing: a cardboard archive box, soft with age, with two letters written on the lid in faded ink. O.L. And underneath, smaller: 1972-73.

The box was full of paper. Most of it was carbon copies, thin as onion skin, covered in typing. Portuguese translations, she realised, of English texts. She recognised the famous first lines of a novel by Dickens, a speech from Hamlet, something by Oscar Wilde, and then pages that were not literature at all: a translation of an article from a British newspaper about political prisoners, a text about freedom of the press. Some of the pages had been typed so small that they could be folded and hidden inside a book.
Then she saw the mark.
It was in the bottom right-hand corner of almost every page: a tiny printer's stamp, no bigger than a fingernail, of a sparrow inside a circle.

Inês knew that sparrow. She had known it all her life. It was stamped on the wooden box where her grandfather kept his composing stick, on the inside cover of every book on his shelf, on the birthday cards he still made for her every year, even with his shaking hands. Her grandfather had told her once that his own father had chosen the sparrow because it was small, ordinary and impossible to keep in a cage.

Under the carbon copies there was a sheet of writing paper, water-stained, the ink run into pale blue clouds. Only some words were legible: told me that... gave them our names... cannot... Thursday. And under that, a small folded note, in English, in a hurried hand:
J., if anything happens to me, burn everything. Do not try to find me. E.

Her hands were cold. She took out her phone and photographed everything: the box, the sparrow, the stained page, the note. Then, without really thinking, she sent the photos to Tomás with three words: "Look at this."
She was putting the note back in the box when she heard it. A key, in the front door.
Daniel had said he would not be back until Monday. Margaret Hale was on a train to Lisbon.
The door opened, and footsteps crossed the main office towards the back room.

chapters.title: Two Letters
paragraphs: It was Margaret Hale. Her coat was wet and she was carrying her umbrella like a weapon.

"The trains are on strike," she said. "Nobody told me, naturally. I came back to collect my notes and..." She stopped in the doorway of the back room. She looked at the open drawer, then at the box on the table, then at the folded note in Inês's hand.
For a few seconds neither of them moved. Somewhere below, a scooter went past, and the windows trembled.
"Did you read it?" said Margaret.

Inês could have lied. She had a story half ready: the drawer had been open, she had only wanted to close it, the box had fallen. But Margaret Hale was looking at her with an expression she had not seen before, not anger exactly, more like someone waiting for a diagnosis, and the story died before she opened her mouth.
"Yes. I read it. I'm sorry. The drawer was open, but that's not an excuse. I shouldn't have touched anything."

"No. You shouldn't." Margaret took the note from her, very gently, and put it back in the box. "In this profession, Ms Carvalho, there is one thing that matters more than talent, and it is not speed and it is not grammar. It is discretion. A translator reads people's divorces, their illnesses, their bank statements, their secrets. If we cannot be trusted with a drawer, we cannot be trusted with anything."
"That sparrow," said Inês, "is my grandfather's mark."
Margaret Hale closed her eyes for a moment. Then she pulled out a chair, sat down in her wet coat and said, "Yes. I know."

She told it the way she corrected documents: precisely, without decoration. Her father, Edward Hale, had come to Porto in the nineteen-fifties to work for one of the British port wine firms in Vila Nova de Gaia. He had been a quiet, bookish man who read Dickens on the ferry and argued with the Portuguese censors in his head. At that time, she explained, Portugal had been a dictatorship for decades. Newspapers were censored, books were banned, and the political police, which everyone still called the PIDE, although it had changed its name by then, watched anyone who asked too many questions.

"In 1972 my father joined a small group. A printer, three university students and an Englishman who could get books from London. They called themselves Os Leitores. The Readers." Margaret touched the letters on the lid of the box. "They translated things that people here were not allowed to read, and the printer printed them, small, so that they could be hidden inside ordinary books. Novels, poems, articles. Nothing violent. Words."
"And the printer was my grandfather."

"The printer was your grandfather. In March 1973 the police arrested him and the three students on the same night. A few days later my father was told he had forty-eight hours to leave the country. He was not arrested, because he was British and that would have been inconvenient for everybody. He was simply expelled. I was fourteen. We left with two suitcases, and I never said goodbye to anyone at school."
"But why did he think..." Inês stopped. "The note says, if anything happens, burn everything."

"He wrote that note for your grandfather, and he never managed to give it to him. The police were faster." Margaret looked at the window, where the rain was running down in long lines. "My father never spoke about Porto again, not once, until the night before he died, in 1990. He was very ill. He took my hand and said: 'The printer talked, Meg. They told me so. I didn't want to believe it, but I'm sure of it now.' Those were almost his last words."
"My grandfather would never..."

"You can't know that. You weren't born. Nor was your mother, probably." It was not said unkindly. "I came back to Porto in 1981 because I wanted to understand. A colleague of my father's had hidden this box in a wine lodge for eight years. I opened this agency, I learnt to live here again, and I never once went to Miragaia to knock on your grandfather's door. When you said his name in September, I thought: I do not want his granddaughter in my office. The next day I thought that was unfair. You are not your grandfather, and I am not my father." She stood up. "Now I'm not sure I was right to give you the benefit of the doubt."

Inês went home in the rain without an umbrella. She did not tell Margaret about the photographs she had sent to Tomás. Later she would ask herself why, and the only honest answer was that she had been ashamed enough for one day.

On Monday she wrote Margaret a letter, on paper, the way Daniel had once been made to. It took her four drafts. Dear Ms Hale, I am writing to apologise for my behaviour on Saturday. I fully understand that I overstepped the limits of my position and that my actions were a serious breach of confidentiality. Although I cannot undo what happened, I would like to assure you that it will not happen again. Should you decide to end my contract, I will of course accept your decision. Yours sincerely, Inês Carvalho.
Margaret read it in front of her on Saturday morning, folded it once and put it in her drawer. "Your connectors have improved," she said. "Daniel needs coffee." And that was all. Inês kept the job.

November was the month of tests. Inês revised verb tenses at the kitchen table while her grandfather listened to the news and her mother slept. She watched him more carefully now. She noticed how he always sat facing the door. She noticed that he never answered the phone before the third ring and never signed anything without reading it twice. Once she asked him, as if it were part of her History homework, what he remembered about the years before the revolution.

"I remember that you had to be careful what you said in cafés," he said. "And that there were things a man could read in Paris that he could go to prison for reading in Porto." He went back to his newspaper. "You should revise. You've got Philosophy tomorrow."

Christmas came. On the twenty-fourth they had salt cod and boiled potatoes and cabbage, as every Portuguese family has done for longer than anyone can remember, and a bolo-rei that her mother had bought on the way home from the hospital, and her grandfather found the little broad bean in his slice, which meant that he would have to buy the cake next year. He laughed so much that he had to take off his glasses. Inês could not remember when she had last heard him laugh like that.

At one in the morning, when everyone was asleep, she went to his desk to find the sticky tape for the last present. That was what she told herself. The tape was in the top drawer. She did not need to open the second drawer, or the third, or to lift the folder of old electricity bills at the bottom of the third.

Under the folder there was an envelope, yellow with age, stamped but never posted. It was addressed, in her grandfather's careful capitals, to MR EDWARD HALE, LONDON, with no street and no number, as if he had not known where to send it, or had not wanted to know.

The envelope was not sealed. Inside there was a single sheet, written in English, an English that had been learnt slowly and with great effort. It was dated the twentieth of May, 1974, less than a month after the revolution.

Edward, I am free now. Everyone is free now. But I cannot be free of one thing. For nine days I said nothing. On the tenth day they showed me your letter. Your handwriting, Edward. Your signature. I have read it a thousand times in my head since then, and I still do not understand why you did it.
