chapters.title: Recalled to Life
paragraphs: Not until the house was completely silent did Inês dare to put the letter back. She slid it into the envelope, the envelope under the folder, the folder under the bills, and closed the drawer as if it were made of glass. Then she lay awake until the trams started running.

It was the symmetry that frightened her. In a grey cabinet on Rua das Flores, an Englishman had left his daughter one sentence: the printer talked. In a drawer two kilometres away, a printer had kept a letter for fifty years that said the opposite: the Englishman talked. What she could not understand was how two people could each be so sure, and how at least one of them had to be wrong.

"Or both," said Tomás, when she told him on the first day of the second term. They were sitting on the wall outside school, eating chestnuts from a paper cone. "Maybe they both talked. People do, under pressure. Look, I've still got your photos. There are tools now that can restore damaged documents. You feed in the stained page, the AI predicts the missing words, and..."
"No."
"I'm only saying..."
"Tomás. Those photos are not mine. They're not yours either. Delete them."
He held up both hands. "Fine. Relax." Later she would remember that he had said fine, and that he had not said deleted.

Having spent the whole holiday with the two letters going round in her head, Inês found it strange to sit in English class on Monday and listen to Professora Matos talking about Charles Dickens as if he were just a name on the syllabus.

"'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times,'" Professora Matos read from the board. "The opening of A Tale of Two Cities, published in 1859. London and Paris, the French Revolution. Dickens is writing about a terrible moment in history, but notice what he does: he refuses to choose. Best and worst at the same time. Rarely does a first sentence tell you so clearly how to read a whole book." She tapped the board. "The first part of the novel is called 'Recalled to Life'. A man who has been in prison for eighteen years is brought back into the world. Can a person who has lived in the dark for so long ever really come back? That is your essay question."

Inês wrote it down and thought about her grandfather sitting with his back to the wall in every café. Thirteen months, her mother had once said, by accident, and then refused to say thirteen months of what. Inês had always assumed it was an illness. Now she was no longer sure of anything.

At the agency, January was busy. A cleaning company needed its contracts in English, a hotel in the Ribeira wanted its menus translated before the tourists returned, and on the third Saturday Daniel took her with him to a meeting at the parish council in Bonfim.

"Pro bono," he explained on the way. "Which means free, which means Margaret pretends she doesn't know about it. There are eight men from Nepal sharing a two-bedroom flat. The landlord wants them out by March, but they've got a contract until December. Most of them speak good English. The landlord speaks Portuguese and football. We're in the middle."

The meeting room smelt of radiator dust and old coffee. The landlord, a heavy man in a leather jacket, spoke fast and looked mostly at the ceiling. The eight tenants sat in a row, polite and very still, and their spokesman, a former schoolteacher called Bishal, answered every question in careful, formal English that made Inês think of Margaret's letters. Daniel interpreted the landlord; Inês interpreted the tenants. For forty minutes it went well. At the end, Bishal asked whether the landlord would repair the broken boiler before the winter got worse.
"Logo se vê," said the landlord, standing up and zipping his jacket.
"He says, 'We'll see,'" Inês translated, and Bishal smiled, nodded and thanked him warmly.
Only when they were outside in the cold did Daniel stop her. "You translated it correctly," he said. "Word for word. But what did he mean?"

Inês felt her face go hot. Every Portuguese person over the age of six knew what "logo se vê" meant. It meant no. It meant: don't ask me again. And Bishal, who had lived in Porto for two years and in Kathmandu for thirty, had heard a promise.

They went back in. It took twenty awkward minutes, a phone call to a lawyer and the president of the parish council, but by the end the landlord had agreed, in writing, to repair the boiler by the end of the month.

Bishal shook her hand at the door. "Thank you for going back," he said. "In my language, too, there are many ways to say no without saying it. At home I would have heard it at once. But when you live in a foreign language, you get tired, and a tired man hears what he hopes." He smiled. "Next time I will ask you what the Portuguese really mean."

"Don't feel bad," said Daniel, as they walked down towards the river. "Words are the easy part. What's hard is everything people don't say." He pushed his hands into his pockets. "My parents are from Lagos. I was born in London. When I go to Nigeria, my cousins call me 'the English boy'. In London, people ask me where I'm really from. Here in Porto, everybody calls me 'o inglês'. I used to think I had to choose. Now I think being from three places is like speaking three languages. You don't lose anything. You just hear more."
"Do you ever feel at home?"
He laughed. "Home is wherever I've left my phone charger." Then, more seriously: "And wherever someone notices when you've understood something wrong. Like you just did."

That night Inês opened the photos on her laptop, not because she had a plan, but because she could not stop herself. She went through them slowly: the box, the note, the stained page, and then the carbon copies, one by one. On the fourth image, a translation of the first chapter of A Tale of Two Cities, something caught her eye. She zoomed in. Then she zoomed in again.

Some of the letters were not on the line. They sat a fraction higher than the others, a millimetre, perhaps less, as if the typist had pressed a key at the exact moment the paper moved. On an old manual typewriter, she knew, you could do that deliberately, by turning the roller half a line. Her grandfather had shown her once, when she was nine, laughing, as a trick for writing secret birthday messages.

Taking a pencil and the back of her Philosophy notes, she began to copy the raised letters in order. At first they made no sense. Then they made Portuguese, without accents, because accents do not climb:
A L G U E M D E D E N T R O L E A S N O S S A S C A R T A S
Alguém de dentro lê as nossas cartas. Someone on the inside is reading our letters.
She checked it three times. She checked the next page, and the next, and found more raised letters, which spelled only a date: 14 3 73. The fourteenth of March, 1973.
Two days before the arrests.

Inês sat back from the screen. There had been five Readers: an Englishman, a printer and three students. One of them had been her grandfather. One of them had been Margaret Hale's father. And one of them, according to a message hidden in Dickens fifty-three years ago, had been reading the others' letters.

chapters.title: The Readiness Is All
paragraphs: What Inês did next was the hardest thing she had done all year, harder than any exam. On the first Saturday of February, she waited until Daniel had gone out for lunch, knocked on the door of the back office and put her laptop on Margaret Hale's desk.
"I have to tell you two things," she said. "And you're not going to like either of them."

She told her about the photographs: that she had taken them in October, before Margaret came back in the rain, and that she had never confessed. Then, before she could lose her courage, she told her about the envelope in her grandfather's drawer, and showed her the photo she had taken of that letter too, because by now she had stopped pretending to be a person who did not take photos of other people's secrets.
Margaret read her grandfather's letter twice. When she reached the words "your signature", her hand moved to the chain around her neck and gripped it.

"That is not possible," she said. "My father was told that the printer had confessed. The officer who expelled him said so. He said, 'Your friend Carvalho has been very helpful.' My father repeated those words to me on his deathbed."
"And my grandfather was shown a letter in your father's handwriting."
They looked at each other across the desk. Not once in the months she had worked there had Inês seen Margaret Hale look uncertain. She looked uncertain now.
"Then somebody lied," Margaret said slowly. "To one of them. Or to both."
"There's something else." Inês opened the photo of the carbon copy and showed her the raised letters, and then her pencil notes. Alguém de dentro lê as nossas cartas. 14 3 73.

Margaret said nothing for a long time. Then she took off her glasses, rubbed her eyes and laughed, a short, surprised laugh with no pleasure in it. "Oscar Wilde was right. 'The truth is rarely pure and never simple.' My father used to say that every time I asked him a straight question. I thought he was being clever. Perhaps he was being honest."

They worked on it that afternoon and long after the office should have closed, with the real box open on the desk and the lamps on. Margaret made tea in a brown teapot, the British way, with milk, and Inês drank it to be polite and then asked whether there was any coffee.

"You see, that is the whole problem with this city," said Margaret, almost smiling. "I grew up here, at the British school, playing tennis at the Cricket Club on Sundays, drinking tea at five o'clock while all my Portuguese friends were drinking strong black coffee. At school in England, after we left, the girls called me 'the Portuguese one' because I kissed people on both cheeks and ate dinner at nine. Here, people still call me 'a inglesa' after forty-five years. Hardly had I learnt to be one thing when I was told I was the other." She put the cup down. "Daniel says it's an advantage. On good days, I believe him."

Turning over the carbon copies one by one, they found more raised letters: dates, times and, three times, the same phrase in English, typed at the top of a page as if it were a title. The readiness is all.

"Hamlet," said Margaret at once. "Act Five. Hamlet knows he may die, and he says that what matters is not when it comes, but to be ready for it." She was quiet for a moment. "It was a signal. I'm almost sure of it now. Sometimes, on a Thursday, my father would come home and say at dinner, 'The readiness is all, Meg,' and then go out again after I'd gone to bed. I thought it was a joke between us. It was a meeting."
"Who were the others? The three students?"

"I don't know. My father never told me their names. That was the rule: each person knew as few names as possible, so that nobody could give away more than a little." Margaret looked at the photo of the raised letters. "Only one person alive knows who they were."

Inês walked home along the river that night, past the cafés of the Ribeira where tourists were photographing the lights of Gaia on the black water. Somewhere on the other side, behind the big illuminated names of the port wine lodges, a colleague of Edward Hale's had hidden a cardboard box for eight years. Somewhere on this side, in a workshop that no longer existed, her grandfather had turned a roller half a line and typed a warning that nobody had understood. Never before had the city looked so beautiful to her, or so full of things it had decided not to say.

So it was not until the following Tuesday evening, after her mother had left for her night shift, that Inês sat down opposite her grandfather at the kitchen table and told him everything. The job. The box with the sparrow. Margaret Hale. The drawer, the letter, the photographs. She had prepared it like a speech for the debate club, and it came out in the wrong order anyway.
Her grandfather listened without moving. Only when she reached the part about his drawer did something change in his face, and she would have preferred him to shout.
"You opened my drawer," he said. "You read my letter. And you showed it to her. To his daughter."

"I'm sorry. I know I shouldn't have. But Avô, she thinks you betrayed her father. And you think he betrayed you. And I think..." She pushed the paper with the decoded message across the table. "I think somebody wanted you both to think that."

Not knowing what else to do, she watched him read it. He read the Portuguese words, and then the date, and his hands, which always trembled a little, began to shake so badly that he had to put the paper down.

"I typed that," he said. "On the Olivetti, in the workshop, with the door locked. Edward said I was being dramatic. He said that in his country nobody opened other people's letters." He made a sound that was not quite a laugh. "He loved this country, but he never understood it. Or perhaps he understood it better than I did. I don't know any more."
"You did? Then who was it? Who was reading your letters? Was it one of the students?"
He looked at her for a long moment, as if he were trying to decide how old she was. Then he stood up, took his coat from the hook, and said, in a voice she had never heard him use, "Go to bed, Inês."
"Go to bed."
She heard him go out. She heard the street door. She lay awake until two, until she heard the key in the lock again and his slow steps in the corridor, and then, without meaning to, she fell asleep.

When she woke up, the flat was too quiet. There was no radio. His bed was made, the way he made it in the army, so tight you could bounce a coin on it. On the kitchen table, under the sugar bowl, there was a note in his careful capitals, in Portuguese.
Fui a Lisboa. Devia ter feito isto há cinquenta anos. Não te preocupes.
I've gone to Lisbon. I should have done this fifty years ago. Don't worry.
His phone was on the table beside the note, switched off.

chapters.title: Two Cities
paragraphs: It was her mother who understood first. She read the note standing in the kitchen in her hospital uniform, still smelling of disinfectant, and sat down slowly on the nearest chair.

"Torre do Tombo," she said. "The national archive. That's where the files of the political police are kept. People can ask to see their own." She looked at the note again. "In fifty years he has never wanted to know what they wrote about him. Never. What did you say to him, Inês?"
So Inês told her mother too, everything, for the second time in two days, and her mother did not shout either. She just said, "I'm on duty until eight tonight. I can't go. Somebody has to go."

Somebody turned out to be Inês and Daniel, because when Inês phoned the agency to say that she would not be in on Saturday, it was Daniel who answered, and Daniel who said, "Campanhã, the 8.39 train. I'll buy the tickets. Don't argue." Margaret did not come. "He won't want to see me," she said on the phone, and for once her voice was not quite steady. "Not yet. Bring him home, Inês."

Having slept for about three hours, Inês spent most of the trip staring at the fields and the eucalyptus trees going past, while Daniel answered emails and pretended not to watch her. Somewhere after Coimbra he put his laptop away.

"My grandmother lived through a military government in Nigeria," he said. "Not the same as here, not the same at all, but she used to say a thing I didn't understand until I was older. She said the worst part was not the soldiers. It was learning to be careful. She said you could take away the soldiers in a day, but it took a whole life to stop being careful." He shrugged. "Maybe your grandfather is still being careful."

The Torre do Tombo was enormous, a pale, heavy building that looked more like a fortress than a library, standing at the end of a wide avenue near the university. Inside it was quiet and cool and smelt of floor polish. They found him in the entrance hall, sitting very straight on a bench with his hat on his knees, like a man waiting to see a doctor.
He did not seem surprised to see her. He looked at Daniel for a long moment.
"You work for her," he said in English. His English was slow and old-fashioned, and some of the words came out with the stress in unexpected places, but it was clear.
"I do, sir. Daniel Okafor."
"Okafor." Her grandfather tried the name carefully, as if he were setting it in type. "You are not English."
"I'm from London. My parents are from Nigeria. It's a long story."

"All the good stories are." Her grandfather almost smiled. Then he turned to Inês. "I have filled in the forms. A very kind young woman explained everything. They must find the file, and prepare it, and protect the names of other people who are in it. It will take some weeks. Then I will come back, and I will read it." He put his hat on. "I have waited fifty years. I can wait a few weeks."

They had lunch in a small restaurant near Campo Grande, grilled fish and salad and a jug of house wine that her grandfather drank and Inês and Daniel did not. And there, with the plates pushed aside and the waiter shouting orders in the background, Joaquim Carvalho told the story for the first time in his life.

They had come for him at four in the morning, on the sixteenth of March, 1973. He remembered that it was raining and that he had not had time to put on socks. They had taken him to the police headquarters in Porto, on Rua do Heroísmo, where for nine days and nine nights they did not let him sleep. Each time he closed his eyes, someone shouted, or banged on a table, or made him stand up. Never once did they hit him, he said, as if that were important to say; they did not need to. After the fourth day, he could no longer tell which voices were real.

"And on the tenth day, a man in a grey suit sat down in front of me, very polite, and put a letter on the table. In English. In Edward's handwriting. It talked about the Thursdays, and the printer in Miragaia, and the books. There was his signature at the bottom. The man said, 'Your English friend has told us everything. Why are you still protecting him?'" Her grandfather turned his glass round on the tablecloth. "I said nothing. Not then, not afterwards. But something in me broke that day, and it did not mend."

They sent him to the prison at Caxias, near Lisbon, for thirteen months. On the night of the twenty-sixth of April, 1974, the gates were opened, and crowds outside were shouting and singing and throwing carnations, and he walked out into it and did not feel anything at all.
"Everyone was celebrating," he said. "I was free, and all I could think was: Edward. Why?"
"Did you ever write to him?" asked Inês. "Apart from the letter in your drawer?"
"I didn't have his address. And I was proud. Then I heard he had died, in England, years later. So that was that."
Daniel had been silent all this time. Now he asked, quietly, "What was he like? Before?"

Her grandfather's face changed. "He taught me English. Did you know that? With Dickens. A Tale of Two Cities. We read it together in the workshop, one page every Thursday, with a dictionary. He loved the end, where Sydney Carton goes to the guillotine in place of another man. He used to read the last lines aloud, and he would always cry, the fool, every single time. 'It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done.'" He stopped. "Such a sentimental man. That's why I never understood. He was the kind of man who cries at the end of a book. Not the kind who signs a letter to the police."
"Then perhaps he didn't," said Inês.
Her grandfather looked at her. "That is what I came here to find out."

On the train home he fell asleep almost immediately, his head against the window, his hat on his knees. Inês watched the light go orange and then grey over the fields. She felt, for the first time in months, almost calm. Whatever the file said, at least now they would know.
Her phone buzzed. Then it buzzed again, and again, and kept buzzing. Tomás.
"ines please dont be angry"
"i did something stupid"
"i ran the stained page through the restoration tool, just to see, i swear i only posted it in a history group with like 200 people"
"someone shared it"
"have you seen instagram"

Below the messages was a link. It opened onto a post by an account called Porto Esquecido, which had a hundred and twenty thousand followers. The image was the water-stained page from the box, but clean now, sharp, every gap filled in by the machine in neat, convincing handwriting. Inês read the sentence in the middle and felt the train tilt under her.
They told me that Joaquim Carvalho gave them our names. I cannot forgive him for Thursday.
The post had been shared eleven thousand times. Under it, the first comment said: "Finally the truth about the traitor of Miragaia."

chapters.title: Filling the Gaps
paragraphs: Inês did not tell her grandfather on the train. She told herself that she was letting him sleep. The truth was that she did not know how to say it, and that she hoped, stupidly, that the post would somehow disappear before morning.

It did not disappear. By Monday it had been shared thirty thousand times, and the comments had spread from Instagram to every place where people in Porto argue with strangers. Some people wrote that it was fake. Many more wrote that they had always suspected it. Someone found a photograph of the Readers' printer in an old newspaper from May 1974: a thin young man with dark hair, walking out of Caxias among the carnations. Someone else found the address of the building in Miragaia where the workshop had been. Nobody, as far as Inês could see, found the address of the truth.
She met Tomás after school on the steps of the library. He looked as if he had not slept either.

"I didn't invent anything," he said, before she could speak. "I want you to know that. The tool doesn't invent. It looks at the visible words, the shape of the ink, the context, and it predicts what's most likely to be there. It's trained on millions of documents. It's supposed to be ninety-something per cent accurate."
"It filled a gap with my grandfather's name."

"Because the context made it probable! The letter was in a box about him, it was written by the man who..." He stopped. "Look. I labelled it. In the original post I wrote 'AI reconstruction, not verified'. That account cut the label off when they shared it. That's not my fault."
"Whose fault is it, then?"
"Theirs! The platform's! Everyone's!" He ran his hands through his hair. "If they hadn't cropped it, nobody would have taken it seriously."

"If you'd deleted the photos when I asked you, nobody would have seen it at all." She heard her own voice, very cold, very like Margaret Hale's. "And if I hadn't sent them to you in the first place, we wouldn't be having this conversation. I know. I'm not pretending I'm innocent."

Tomás was silent for a while. Then he said, more quietly: "I wrote to the account. They said that historical documents belong to everyone, and that they had a right to share them. I reported the post to the platform. They replied that it didn't break their community guidelines."
"Then post a correction. Say that you made it. Say that the words aren't real."

He looked away, at the students coming out of the gym. "I've applied for the scholarship. The one for Computer Science in Lisbon, the one I told you about. Do you know what my application essay is about?" He laughed, without any humour. "Responsible artificial intelligence. If they find out that I'm the guy who started this, I can forget it. Supposing I did post a correction, who would even read it? Thirty thousand people have shared the lie. Maybe two hundred would see the truth."
"So you'd rather do nothing."
"I'd rather not ruin my life for something that's already happened."
She left him on the steps. It was the first time in eleven years of friendship that she walked away from Tomás without saying goodbye.

At school, Professora Matos had, by coincidence or not, chosen the same week to start the unit on ethics and technology. She wrote a question on the board in her neat, slanting handwriting: Should artificial intelligence be allowed to reconstruct damaged historical documents? The class split down the middle. Some argued that the technology could save documents that would otherwise be lost forever. Others argued that a reconstruction was only a guess dressed up as a fact. A girl called Beatriz, who never spoke, said that the problem was not the machine but the people who stopped asking questions once a machine had given them an answer, and the class went quiet for a moment.
Tomás sat at the back and said nothing at all.

At home, her grandfather found out the way old people find out everything now: from a neighbour. Dona Fátima from the second floor stopped him on the stairs, holding her phone, and asked whether it was true, what they were saying on the internet. Inês found him an hour later sitting at the kitchen table with her mother's tablet, reading the comments one by one, very slowly, with his finger on the screen.
"Avô, don't. Please. They don't know anything."

"Traitor," he read aloud. "Coward. Shame on his family." He turned the tablet face down. "Fifty years ago, they put me in a room and told me lies until I couldn't tell what was real. Now they don't even need the room." He stood up. "I'm going to lie down."
He did not go to the café the next day, or the day after. He had gone to the same café at the same time every morning for twenty years.

Margaret Hale was not at the agency on Saturday. Daniel said that she had taken a few days off, that she had been phoned by journalists, and that she had not looked well. "She's not answering me either," he said. "I've never seen her switch her phone off. She sleeps with it under her pillow in case a client in Australia needs a comma."

They worked in silence for a while. Then Daniel put down his pen. "Can I ask you something difficult? Have you thought about what happens if the file says he did it? If he really talked, in the end, after all those nights without sleep?"

Inês had thought about nothing else. "If he had talked," she said slowly, "it would be because they broke him. That's not the same as betraying someone. And even if the file said that, he would still be my grandfather. Were it not for him, I'd never have learnt to read backwards." She tried to smile. "But it won't say that. It can't."
"Then you'll have to wait for the paper to prove it," said Daniel. "Not the machine."

On the morning of the twenty-fifth of April, Inês went down to the Avenida dos Aliados with her mother. Her grandfather refused to come. Every year since she was a child they had gone together, all three of them, to watch the parade and buy red carnations from the women with buckets at the corner, and every year he had bought one for her and one for her mother and none for himself. This year he stayed in his room with the door closed.

The avenue was full: families with pushchairs, old men with medals, students with banners about housing and climate and the minimum wage, a brass band playing a little too slowly. Her mother bought two carnations. Inês held hers and tried to feel what she was supposed to feel.

At the kiosk on the corner, the national newspapers were hanging on clips in the sun. She saw the photograph before she saw the headline: the thin young man with dark hair, walking out of Caxias among the carnations. Above it, in large black letters:
THE TRAITOR WHO WAS GIVEN A CARNATION
And underneath, in smaller letters, a quotation, in Portuguese, that Inês read three times before she could believe it:
"My father believed it until the day he died," says Margaret Hale, daughter of the expelled Englishman.

chapters.title: Setting the Record Straight
paragraphs: Margaret Hale lived on the top floor of an old house in Foz, with a view of the lighthouse and the grey Atlantic. It took her a long time to answer the door. She was wearing a cardigan buttoned up wrong, and she looked ten years older than she had in March.
"I know why you're here," she said. "Come in. Please."

Inês had rehearsed a speech on the bus. It was angry and well organised, with three arguments and a conclusion, and it disappeared completely when she saw the kitchen table. It was covered with papers: copies of emails to the newspaper, printouts, a dictionary, and in the middle, in a plastic sleeve, the water-stained page from the box.

"The journalist rang me on the twenty-second," said Margaret. "He asked me whether my father had believed that the printer betrayed him. I said, 'My father believed it until the day he died. But I no longer do, and I have good reasons.' He thanked me very politely." She picked up a printout of the article and let it fall. "They used the first sentence. Not the second. Every word they printed is true, and the whole thing is a lie."
"Did you ask them to correct it?"

"Three times. The editor replied that they had reported my words accurately. Which they had." Margaret sat down. "I spent forty years translating other people's words, Inês. I know better than anyone that you can betray someone without changing a single word. All you have to do is choose which ones to keep."
Then she pushed the plastic sleeve across the table, next to a large photograph.

"I took it to a conservation laboratory at the university in Lisbon, the week after the post appeared. Ink that has faded can sometimes be seen again under infrared light. It's an old technique; it was used long before anyone had heard of artificial intelligence. They sent me this yesterday."
The photograph showed the same page, but darker, strange, like an X-ray. And across it, perfectly legible, in Edward Hale's elegant handwriting:
They told me that J. gave them our names. I cannot believe it. I will not believe it until I hear it from him, and they will not let me see him. They say I must leave by Thursday.
Inês read it twice. "I cannot believe it," she said. "Not 'I cannot forgive him'."

"He didn't believe it." Margaret's voice was very low. "Not in 1973. It took him seventeen years of silence in a small town in Surrey to start believing it. Had he been able to speak to your grandfather even once, it would never have happened. But nobody was allowed to speak to anybody. That was the whole point."
They sat for a while without talking. A ship's horn sounded somewhere out on the sea.

"There is something else," said Margaret. "Your grandfather has a right of reply. It is in the Constitution. A newspaper which publishes something about a person has to publish that person's answer. He doesn't need my permission, and he doesn't need a lawyer. He just needs to write it."

That evening Inês sat with her grandfather at the kitchen table, as they had sat over her homework for years, but this time she held the pen. He dictated in Portuguese and she wrote, and every so often he stopped and asked her to read a sentence back, and changed one word, the way a printer corrects a proof. It was not an angry letter. It was very short. It said that he had been arrested on the sixteenth of March 1973, that he had spent nine days without sleep and thirteen months in prison, that he had never given any names, and that he had requested his file from the national archive so that anyone who wished could read the truth in the police's own words. It ended: I was not given a carnation. I walked past them. I did not think I deserved one, because I had lost a friend. I am beginning to think that the friend was lost to me by the same people who arrested me.
The newspaper published it the following Saturday, on page seven.
That week Tomás came to see her. He stood in the doorway of the flat with his hands in his pockets and did not come in.

"I've done it," he said. "I've posted a video. I explain everything. How I got the photos, how the tool works, which words were really on the page and which words the machine made up. I show the infrared image, if Ms Hale lets me. I say that it was my fault and nobody else's." He swallowed. "And I've written to the scholarship people and told them. Before they found out from someone else."
"What did they say?"

"Nothing yet. But at least I have set the record straight." He shrugged, badly. "If I lose it, I lose it. I kept thinking that if I didn't own up, I'd be exactly like that account. Or the newspaper. Everybody saying, it's not my fault, I only shared it." He looked at her for the first time. "I'm sorry, Inês. To you and to him. Mostly to him."

The video was not shared thirty thousand times. It was shared about four thousand times, which Tomás said was a disaster and Professora Matos said was four thousand more than most corrections ever get. Beatriz showed it in class as part of her presentation on accountability in technology. Somebody at the national newspaper must have seen it too, because the following week, at the bottom of page twelve, a small box appeared, headed Clarification.
Then, on a Tuesday in the middle of May, a letter arrived from the Torre do Tombo. The file was ready to be consulted.
Her grandfather read the letter in the hall, still in his coat, and then said something that surprised everyone.
"I will not read it without a Hale in the room."

So on the last Saturday of May, four people took the early train to Lisbon: an old printer in his best suit, an Englishwoman in a hat she had not worn for years, a student who should have been revising for her exams, and a project manager who had told his clients he was ill.

The meeting at Campanhã station was the most awkward ten minutes of Inês's life. Margaret and her grandfather shook hands like diplomats from two countries at war. For the first hour they talked about the weather. Somewhere after Pombal, her grandfather looked at Margaret for a long time and said, in his slow English, "You have his eyebrows."
"I know," said Margaret. "I've always hated them."
And her grandfather laughed, the way he had laughed at Christmas over the broad bean in the bolo-rei, and something in the carriage changed.

The reading room at the archive was silent and cool, with long tables and green lamps. A young archivist brought a grey cardboard folder tied with string and placed it in front of Joaquim Carvalho with great care, as if it might still be dangerous. On the cover, in old-fashioned type, was his name, and a number.
He untied the string with his trembling hands. Nobody offered to help him.

The first page was a typed summary, in the dry language of the police: name, date of birth, profession, address. And then, halfway down, a line that made Margaret Hale take hold of the edge of the table.
Origem da informação. Source of information.
And after it, typed neatly, in capital letters, a name that all four of them knew.
EDWARD HALE.

chapters.title: A Far, Far Better Thing
paragraphs: Nobody spoke. Margaret Hale's knuckles had gone white on the edge of the table. Her grandfather sat completely still, looking at the name, and Inês saw that he was not surprised. He had been shown that name before, fifty-three years ago, by a man in a grey suit.
It was Daniel who reached out, very gently, and turned the page.

Behind the summary was a photograph of a letter, slightly blurred, with a rubber stamp across the top: CORRESPONDÊNCIA INTERCEPTADA. Intercepted correspondence. It was addressed to a Mr Arthur Penrose, a publisher in London, and dated the second of February, 1973. The handwriting was the same elegant hand as on the water-stained page.

Margaret read it aloud, in English, her voice getting quieter with every line. It was not a confession. It was a letter between two old friends. Edward asked Arthur to send more books, "the usual parcel, hidden among the wine catalogues". He wrote that "our Thursday readers" were growing braver. He wrote that "my friend the printer in Miragaia, with his little sparrow" had become a better reader of Dickens than any Englishman he knew. And he wrote that his friend had recently become worried, almost obsessed, that someone was opening their letters. "He sees spies everywhere," Edward had written. "I tell him that in a civilised country nobody reads other people's post. He looks at me as if I were a child."
Clipped to the photograph was a translation into Portuguese, typed by a police translator, with certain words underlined in red: printer, Miragaia, sparrow, Thursday.

"He wrote it the same week," her grandfather said. His voice was steady. "The same week I typed that message in the Dickens. Alguém de dentro lê as nossas cartas. I meant inside the post office. My cousin worked at the sorting office, and he told me that some envelopes were arriving resealed, with the glue still wet. I tried to warn everyone the only way I could." He shook his head slowly. "And Edward thought I was being dramatic, and sat down and wrote to London to say so. And they read it."
Page by page, the rest of the story was put back together in front of them, in the flat, careful language of people who had never imagined that their reports would one day be read by their victims.

There were the interrogation notes. For nine days, it was recorded, the prisoner had refused to answer any questions. On the ninth day an officer had written in the margin that the prisoner "shows no signs of cooperating" and recommended that "he be shown the Englishman's letter, in order to convince him that he has been betrayed". The next entry stated only that the letter had been shown to the prisoner and that he had "remained silent".

There was another note, written in the first days after the arrests, about "the British subject". It was recommended that he should not be arrested, since this "would cause problems with the British consulate and the foreign press". Instead, it was suggested that he be informed that "the printer has confessed", so that he would leave the country quickly and quietly. In the margin, someone had written: Done. He believed it.
And then, at the very back of the folder, there was one more letter.

It was dated the twenty-first of March, 1973, the day before Edward Hale left Portugal. It was written in formal Portuguese, with two small grammatical mistakes that Margaret would correct in her head for the rest of her life. It was addressed to the director of the political police. In it, Edward Hale stated that he alone had organised the group, that he alone had chosen and translated the texts, and that the printer Joaquim Carvalho had only printed what he had been paid to print, without understanding its content. He offered to sign a full confession, and to remain in Portugal and be tried, on one condition: that Joaquim Carvalho and the three students be released.
Across the top of the letter, in pencil, someone had written two words. Sem resposta. No reply.

Margaret Hale broke down. She did it silently, with her hands over her face, the way people do who have been taught all their lives not to make a scene. Inês had never seen an adult cry like that. Daniel put his hand on Margaret's shoulder and kept it there.
Her grandfather read the letter twice. Then he took off his glasses, folded them and put them in his pocket, and said something in Portuguese that Inês did not catch. She leaned closer.

"'It is a far, far better thing that I do,'" he was saying, very softly, in English. "The fool. The sentimental fool. He would have gone to prison for me. And he would have cried at the end of it." He laughed, and his eyes were wet. "He was careless, Margaret. Your father was careless, and brave, and he wrote too many letters. But he was never a traitor."
"Neither were you," said Margaret, through her fingers. "Neither were you. And they made sure that each of you spent the rest of your life believing the other one was."

It was the archivist who finally broke the silence. She had been sitting at a desk at the far end of the room, pretending not to watch, and when she came over she was holding a box of tissues and her own eyes were red.
"I'm sorry," she said. "I've worked here for eleven years. People come and read these files every week. You never get used to it."

They took the last train home. Nobody talked much. Somewhere near Aveiro, Inês woke up from a short sleep and saw that her grandfather and Margaret Hale were sitting side by side, sharing a paper bag of cherries, and talking in a mixture of English and Portuguese about a bookshop on Rua de Santa Catarina that had closed in 1975.

June arrived, and with it the exams. Inês sat her Portuguese exam on a hot morning in a gym that smelt of floor polish and nerves, and when she read the essay question, she almost laughed. It asked about memory, and whether a society has a duty to remember the past. She wrote for an hour without stopping, and she did not mention Joaquim or Edward once, but they were in every line.

Tomás was invited to an interview for the scholarship in Lisbon. They told him that one of the questions would be about his video. He said he was terrified. She said he deserved to be, and then she hugged him, which was the first time since April.

On the night of the twenty-third of June, the night of São João, the whole city went into the streets. Margaret invited everyone to the agency, because, she said, the balcony at the back had the best view of the river in Porto and she had never once used it for a party. Daniel brought grilled sardines on bread from a stall in the street. Inês's mother brought a pot of manjerico and a bag of plastic hammers, and spent the evening hitting everyone on the head with them, which is what you do on São João. Tomás brought nothing and ate everything.
Her grandfather came last. He climbed the three flights of creaking stairs very slowly, and when he arrived he was carrying the old wooden box with the sparrow on the lid.

At midnight the fireworks began over the Douro, and the whole city cheered. While everyone else was looking at the sky, Joaquim Carvalho opened the box, took out his composing stick and, with hands that hardly shook at all, began to set a line of metal letters. It took him a long time. When he had finished, he gave it to Margaret.

She held it up to the light of the fireworks. The letters were reversed, of course, mirror letters, the way they always are before they are printed. Margaret Hale, who had spent her life turning one language into another, read them backwards without any difficulty at all, and then she read them aloud.
"THE READINESS IS ALL."
"Thursday," said Joaquim Carvalho. "Same time as always. I still have half of A Tale of Two Cities to read in English, and my teacher left before we finished."

reading.title: Dear Sir or Madam
text: Inês Carvalho, a seventeen-year-old student in Porto, has applied for a Saturday job at Hale Translations, a small agency run by Margaret Hale, an Englishwoman who was born in Porto. Daniel Okafor, the project manager, has just shown her into Margaret's office.

"Sit down, Ms Carvalho. I have read your CV. It says you are reliable and hard-working. Everybody's CV says that. It is like saying that you have a nose. Tell me something about yourself that isn't true of everyone."
Inês had prepared answers to a dozen questions. This was not one of them. She heard herself say: "I learnt to read from metal letters. Upside down and backwards."

"My grandfather had a printing workshop. The old kind, where you set every letter by hand. When I was small he used to let me make my name in the composing stick. The letters are reversed, so you read them like a mirror. I could read my name backwards before I could read it the right way round." She stopped. "That probably isn't useful for translation."

"On the contrary. Translation is mostly reading things backwards." Ms Hale slid a sheet of paper across the desk. "A client received this from a supplier in Manchester. Translate it into Portuguese for the client's director. You have fifteen minutes."

It was an email, and it was furious. Your lot have completely messed up the brochure. We asked for the blue logo and you've gone and put the green one on five thousand copies. Sort it out by Friday or we're done. Inês read it twice, took a breath and wrote. Margaret Hale read her version in silence, tapping the page with her pen.
"'Your lot'. You have translated it as 'a vossa empresa'. Why?"

"Because the original is rude, but the director doesn't need the rudeness. He needs the information. If I'd translated every word, he might have thought the supplier was insulting him personally. The supplier is angry, but he isn't insulting anybody. He's just from Manchester."

"You could have kept a little more of the anger," said Ms Hale. "'Or we're done' is a threat, and you have made it sound like a suggestion. Clients should know when they are being threatened. However, you have understood the main thing, which most people never do: a translation is not a copy. It is a decision." She put the paper down. "We pay seven euros an hour. You will answer the phone, check documents, make coffee for Daniel, and you will not talk about our clients to anyone. One more question." She took off her glasses and let them drop on their chain. "Your grandfather. The one with the metal letters. What is his name?"
"Joaquim. Joaquim Carvalho. His workshop was in Miragaia, near the river, but he closed it years ago."
"I see," said Ms Hale. She picked up the CV, folded it in half and then in half again. "In that case, Ms Carvalho, I'm afraid I cannot offer you the position."
"Your translation was excellent. This has nothing to do with your translation." Her voice was perfectly polite and perfectly cold. "Daniel will show you out."

reading.title: The Locked Cabinet
text: Inês has accepted a Saturday job at Hale Translations, although her grandfather, Joaquim, asked her to stay away from the agency. Margaret Hale, the owner, first refused to employ her and then changed her mind.

Inês spent two days not deciding. She should have told her grandfather. She knew that. But every time she imagined the conversation, it ended with the door closing without a sound again, so on Wednesday morning she wrote her reply on the bus, deleted "Hi Margaret" three times and finally sent: Dear Ms Hale, Thank you for your email. I am pleased to accept the position and will be at the office on Saturday at 9.00. Kind regards, Inês Carvalho. At dinner she told her family that she had found a Saturday job in an office in the Baixa. It was not a lie. It was simply not the whole truth, and she was surprised how easy it was to say.

By the end of October she had learnt more about professional communication than in five years of English lessons. She had learnt to answer the phone with "Hale Translations, good morning, how may I help you?" without sounding like a robot. She had learnt that you never write "You forgot to send the documents" to a client; you write "It seems that we have not yet received the documents". She had learnt that "Cheers" is acceptable at the end of an email to a translator in Bristol and a disaster at the end of an email to a law firm in Lisbon, because she had made exactly that mistake in her second week.
"Don't worry," Daniel had said. "My first week here I wrote 'Love, Daniel' to a notary. Margaret made me write him a formal letter of apology. By hand."

There were rules, and Margaret explained them on the first day as if she were reading a contract. Clients' names were never mentioned outside the office. Confidential documents, such as medical reports, contracts and asylum papers, were never pasted into online translation tools. "When you put a text into one of those machines," she said, "you don't know where it goes, who reads it, or what it is used for afterwards. Our clients trust us with their lives. Sometimes literally."

The phone did not ring. The office went quiet in that particular way old buildings go quiet, with small noises in the walls. Inês finished checking a contract, filed three invoices in the back room and was turning to leave when she noticed that the top drawer of the grey cabinet was not completely closed. Margaret must have taken something out before leaving for the train and forgotten to turn the key. It was ajar by perhaps a centimetre.
She stood there for a long moment. She could have closed it. She should have closed it. Later she would tell herself that she had meant to close it, and that her hand had simply slipped. It had not.
Inside there was only one thing: a cardboard archive box, soft with age, with two letters written on the lid in faded ink. O.L. And underneath, smaller: 1972-73.

text: One Saturday, alone at the agency, Inês opened a cabinet that was always kept locked and found a box of old papers with her grandfather's printer's mark on them. Margaret Hale, who was supposed to be on a train to Lisbon, has just come back and found her there.

Inês could have lied. She had a story half ready: the drawer had been open, she had only wanted to close it, the box had fallen. But Margaret Hale was looking at her with an expression she had not seen before, not anger exactly, more like someone waiting for a diagnosis, and the story died before she opened her mouth.
"Yes. I read it. I'm sorry. The drawer was open, but that's not an excuse. I shouldn't have touched anything."

"No. You shouldn't." Margaret took the note from her, very gently, and put it back in the box. "In this profession, Ms Carvalho, there is one thing that matters more than talent, and it is not speed and it is not grammar. It is discretion. A translator reads people's divorces, their illnesses, their bank statements, their secrets. If we cannot be trusted with a drawer, we cannot be trusted with anything."

She told it the way she corrected documents: precisely, without decoration. Her father, Edward Hale, had come to Porto in the nineteen-fifties to work for one of the British port wine firms in Vila Nova de Gaia. He had been a quiet, bookish man who read Dickens on the ferry and argued with the Portuguese censors in his head. At that time, she explained, Portugal had been a dictatorship for decades. Newspapers were censored, books were banned, and the political police, which everyone still called the PIDE, although it had changed its name by then, watched anyone who asked too many questions.

"In 1972 my father joined a small group. A printer, three university students and an Englishman who could get books from London. They called themselves Os Leitores. The Readers." Margaret touched the letters on the lid of the box. "They translated things that people here were not allowed to read, and the printer printed them, small, so that they could be hidden inside ordinary books. Novels, poems, articles. Nothing violent. Words."

"The printer was your grandfather. In March 1973 the police arrested him and the three students on the same night. A few days later my father was told he had forty-eight hours to leave the country. He was not arrested, because he was British and that would have been inconvenient for everybody. He was simply expelled. I was fourteen. We left with two suitcases, and I never said goodbye to anyone at school."

"He wrote that note for your grandfather, and he never managed to give it to him. The police were faster." Margaret looked at the window, where the rain was running down in long lines. "My father never spoke about Porto again, not once, until the night before he died, in 1990. He was very ill. He took my hand and said: 'The printer talked, Meg. They told me so. I didn't want to believe it, but I'm sure of it now.' Those were almost his last words."

writing.task: Is it ever acceptable to read someone else's private letters or messages? Write an **opinion text** (120 to 180 words). Give at least two reasons and an example, and use connectors such as *however*, *furthermore* and *therefore*.
writing.model: Most of us would be furious if a friend or a parent read our private messages. Privacy is a basic right, and reading someone's letters without permission is a serious breach of trust. Furthermore, once trust is broken, it is very difficult to rebuild, as Inês discovers when Margaret finds her with the box. However, I believe there are rare situations in which it can be justified. If a parent has strong reasons to think that a child is in danger, for example because a stranger online is threatening them, reading their messages may be the only way to protect them. Similarly, historians read the private letters of people who died long ago, and this helps us understand the past. Even so, these cases should be exceptions, not habits, and the reason must be serious, not simple curiosity. Therefore, my answer is that reading other people's letters is wrong in almost every case, and that anyone who does it should be ready to explain why, and to admit it.

text: In January, Daniel Okafor, the project manager at Hale Translations, takes Inês to a meeting at a parish council in Porto. A group of workers from Nepal are in a dispute with their landlord, and the agency is helping them for free.

"Pro bono," he explained on the way. "Which means free, which means Margaret pretends she doesn't know about it. There are eight men from Nepal sharing a two-bedroom flat. The landlord wants them out by March, but they've got a contract until December. Most of them speak good English. The landlord speaks Portuguese and football. We're in the middle."

The meeting room smelt of radiator dust and old coffee. The landlord, a heavy man in a leather jacket, spoke fast and looked mostly at the ceiling. The eight tenants sat in a row, polite and very still, and their spokesman, a former schoolteacher called Bishal, answered every question in careful, formal English that made Inês think of Margaret's letters. Daniel interpreted the landlord; Inês interpreted the tenants. For forty minutes it went well. At the end, Bishal asked whether the landlord would repair the broken boiler before the winter got worse.
"Logo se vê," said the landlord, standing up and zipping his jacket.
"He says, 'We'll see,'" Inês translated, and Bishal smiled, nodded and thanked him warmly.
Only when they were outside in the cold did Daniel stop her. "You translated it correctly," he said. "Word for word. But what did he mean?"

Inês felt her face go hot. Every Portuguese person over the age of six knew what "logo se vê" meant. It meant no. It meant: don't ask me again. And Bishal, who had lived in Porto for two years and in Kathmandu for thirty, had heard a promise.

They went back in. It took twenty awkward minutes, a phone call to a lawyer and the president of the parish council, but by the end the landlord had agreed, in writing, to repair the boiler by the end of the month.

Bishal shook her hand at the door. "Thank you for going back," he said. "In my language, too, there are many ways to say no without saying it. At home I would have heard it at once. But when you live in a foreign language, you get tired, and a tired man hears what he hopes." He smiled. "Next time I will ask you what the Portuguese really mean."

"Don't feel bad," said Daniel, as they walked down towards the river. "Words are the easy part. What's hard is everything people don't say." He pushed his hands into his pockets. "My parents are from Lagos. I was born in London. When I go to Nigeria, my cousins call me 'the English boy'. In London, people ask me where I'm really from. Here in Porto, everybody calls me 'o inglês'. I used to think I had to choose. Now I think being from three places is like speaking three languages. You don't lose anything. You just hear more."
"Do you ever feel at home?"
He laughed. "Home is wherever I've left my phone charger." Then, more seriously: "And wherever someone notices when you've understood something wrong. Like you just did."

writing.task: "Growing up between two or more cultures is an advantage." Write an **opinion essay** (120 to 180 words). Use examples from your own experience or from the text, and include at least one inversion or cleft sentence.
writing.model: In Portugal today, many teenagers have parents from Brazil, Cape Verde, Ukraine or Nepal, and many Portuguese families have relatives in France or Switzerland. In my opinion, growing up between cultures is mainly an advantage. Not only do these young people often speak two or more languages, but they also learn very early that there is more than one way to see the world. As Daniel says in the story, you do not lose anything; you just hear more. What they develop is a kind of sensitivity: they notice when a "yes" means "no", or when a joke will not work in another country. These skills are useful in any job. However, it is not always easy. Some people feel that they never completely belong anywhere, and they may face prejudice. Even so, I believe that the difficulties are temporary, while the advantages last a lifetime. A person who can move between cultures can also help others understand each other, and our world needs more of those people.

text: Inês has shown Margaret Hale a message hidden in a typed translation of Dickens, "Alguém de dentro lê as nossas cartas" (Someone on the inside is reading our letters), and a 1974 letter where her grandfather accuses Margaret's father of betrayal.

Margaret said nothing for a long time. Then she took off her glasses, rubbed her eyes and laughed, a short, surprised laugh with no pleasure in it. "Oscar Wilde was right. 'The truth is rarely pure and never simple.' My father used to say that every time I asked him a straight question. I thought he was being clever. Perhaps he was being honest."

They worked on it that afternoon and long after the office should have closed, with the real box open on the desk and the lamps on. Margaret made tea in a brown teapot, the British way, with milk, and Inês drank it to be polite and then asked whether there was any coffee.

"You see, that is the whole problem with this city," said Margaret, almost smiling. "I grew up here, at the British school, playing tennis at the Cricket Club on Sundays, drinking tea at five o'clock while all my Portuguese friends were drinking strong black coffee. At school in England, after we left, the girls called me 'the Portuguese one' because I kissed people on both cheeks and ate dinner at nine. Here, people still call me 'a inglesa' after forty-five years. Hardly had I learnt to be one thing when I was told I was the other." She put the cup down. "Daniel says it's an advantage. On good days, I believe him."

Turning over the carbon copies one by one, they found more raised letters: dates, times and, three times, the same phrase in English, typed at the top of a page as if it were a title. The readiness is all.

"Hamlet," said Margaret at once. "Act Five. Hamlet knows he may die, and he says that what matters is not when it comes, but to be ready for it." She was quiet for a moment. "It was a signal. I'm almost sure of it now. Sometimes, on a Thursday, my father would come home and say at dinner, 'The readiness is all, Meg,' and then go out again after I'd gone to bed. I thought it was a joke between us. It was a meeting."

"I don't know. My father never told me their names. That was the rule: each person knew as few names as possible, so that nobody could give away more than a little." Margaret looked at the photo of the raised letters. "Only one person alive knows who they were."

Inês walked home along the river that night, past the cafés of the Ribeira where tourists were photographing the lights of Gaia on the black water. Somewhere on the other side, behind the big illuminated names of the port wine lodges, a colleague of Edward Hale's had hidden a cardboard box for eight years. Somewhere on this side, in a workshop that no longer existed, her grandfather had turned a roller half a line and typed a warning that nobody had understood. Never before had the city looked so beautiful to her, or so full of things it had decided not to say.

Last year two of my friends had a terrible argument, and each told me a completely different story. Both stories were true, in a way, and neither was the whole truth. Only when I listened to both of them did I understand what had really happened. The line also makes me think about the news. Having read a headline, many people think they know everything about a person or an event, when in fact they know only a small part. For me, Wilde's sentence is a reminder to be patient, to ask questions and to accept that some answers are complicated. That is not a weakness. It is a way of being fair.

text: Joaquim Carvalho, Inês's grandfather, has gone to Lisbon to ask for his file from the political police of the dictatorship, kept in the national archive, the Torre do Tombo. Inês and Daniel have found him there. Over lunch, he tells his story for the first time.

They had lunch in a small restaurant near Campo Grande, grilled fish and salad and a jug of house wine that her grandfather drank and Inês and Daniel did not. And there, with the plates pushed aside and the waiter shouting orders in the background, Joaquim Carvalho told the story for the first time in his life.

They had come for him at four in the morning, on the sixteenth of March, 1973. He remembered that it was raining and that he had not had time to put on socks. They had taken him to the police headquarters in Porto, on Rua do Heroísmo, where for nine days and nine nights they did not let him sleep. Each time he closed his eyes, someone shouted, or banged on a table, or made him stand up. Never once did they hit him, he said, as if that were important to say; they did not need to. After the fourth day, he could no longer tell which voices were real.

"And on the tenth day, a man in a grey suit sat down in front of me, very polite, and put a letter on the table. In English. In Edward's handwriting. It talked about the Thursdays, and the printer in Miragaia, and the books. There was his signature at the bottom. The man said, 'Your English friend has told us everything. Why are you still protecting him?'" Her grandfather turned his glass round on the tablecloth. "I said nothing. Not then, not afterwards. But something in me broke that day, and it did not mend."

They sent him to the prison at Caxias, near Lisbon, for thirteen months. On the night of the twenty-sixth of April, 1974, the gates were opened, and crowds outside were shouting and singing and throwing carnations, and he walked out into it and did not feel anything at all.
"Did you ever write to him?" asked Inês. "Apart from the letter in your drawer?"
"I didn't have his address. And I was proud. Then I heard he had died, in England, years later. So that was that."
Daniel had been silent all this time. Now he asked, quietly, "What was he like? Before?"

Her grandfather's face changed. "He taught me English. Did you know that? With Dickens. A Tale of Two Cities. We read it together in the workshop, one page every Thursday, with a dictionary. He loved the end, where Sydney Carton goes to the guillotine in place of another man. He used to read the last lines aloud, and he would always cry, the fool, every single time. 'It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done.'" He stopped. "Such a sentimental man. That's why I never understood. He was the kind of man who cries at the end of a book. Not the kind who signs a letter to the police."
"Then perhaps he didn't," said Inês.
Her grandfather looked at her. "That is what I came here to find out."

writing.model: Governments, banks, schools and technology companies keep enormous amounts of information about us, often without us noticing. In my view, everyone should have the right to see it. First of all, information about a person can change that person's life. A mistake in a file can cost someone a job, a loan or their reputation, and only the person concerned can say whether it is true. Secondly, knowing that people can read their files makes institutions more careful and more honest. reading.title: Filling the Gaps
text: Tomás has used an AI tool to "restore" a damaged letter that Inês photographed. The result accuses her grandfather of betraying his friends, and it has gone viral.
She met Tomás after school on the steps of the library. He looked as if he had not slept either.

"I didn't invent anything," he said, before she could speak. "I want you to know that. The tool doesn't invent. It looks at the visible words, the shape of the ink, the context, and it predicts what's most likely to be there. It's trained on millions of documents. It's supposed to be ninety-something per cent accurate."
"It filled a gap with my grandfather's name."

"Because the context made it probable! The letter was in a box about him, it was written by the man who..." He stopped. "Look. I labelled it. In the original post I wrote 'AI reconstruction, not verified'. That account cut the label off when they shared it. That's not my fault."
"Whose fault is it, then?"
"Theirs! The platform's! Everyone's!" He ran his hands through his hair. "If they hadn't cropped it, nobody would have taken it seriously."

"If you'd deleted the photos when I asked you, nobody would have seen it at all." She heard her own voice, very cold, very like Margaret Hale's. "And if I hadn't sent them to you in the first place, we wouldn't be having this conversation. I know. I'm not pretending I'm innocent."

Tomás was silent for a while. Then he said, more quietly: "I wrote to the account. They said that historical documents belong to everyone, and that they had a right to share them. I reported the post to the platform. They replied that it didn't break their community guidelines."
"Then post a correction. Say that you made it. Say that the words aren't real."

He looked away, at the students coming out of the gym. "I've applied for the scholarship. The one for Computer Science in Lisbon, the one I told you about. Do you know what my application essay is about?" He laughed, without any humour. "Responsible artificial intelligence. If they find out that I'm the guy who started this, I can forget it. Supposing I did post a correction, who would even read it? Thirty thousand people have shared the lie. Maybe two hundred would see the truth."
"So you'd rather do nothing."
"I'd rather not ruin my life for something that's already happened."
She left him on the steps. It was the first time in eleven years of friendship that she walked away from Tomás without saying goodbye.

At school, Professora Matos had, by coincidence or not, chosen the same week to start the unit on ethics and technology. She wrote a question on the board in her neat, slanting handwriting: Should artificial intelligence be allowed to reconstruct damaged historical documents? The class split down the middle. Some argued that the technology could save documents that would otherwise be lost forever. Others argued that a reconstruction was only a guess dressed up as a fact. A girl called Beatriz, who never spoke, said that the problem was not the machine but the people who stopped asking questions once a machine had given them an answer, and the class went quiet for a moment.

writing.model: Artificial intelligence can now create photographs, voices and documents that look completely real. In my opinion, the law should require all of them to be clearly labelled. The first reason is that people trust what they see. Most of us do not have the time or the skills to check where an image comes from, so a label is the simplest protection we have. Had the reconstruction in the story been labelled permanently, inside the image itself, thousands of people would not have believed a lie about an innocent man. Secondly, labels protect history. If AI reconstructions are mixed with real documents, future historians will not know which is which. Some people argue that labels limit creativity or that they are easy to remove. However, a law would make removing them illegal, and creative work would not suffer from being honest about how it was made. Were it not for clear rules, we would soon live in a world where nothing can be trusted. That is too high a price to pay.

reading.title: Setting the Record Straight
text: A national newspaper has presented Joaquim Carvalho as the traitor of a secret group of readers in 1973, quoting Margaret Hale, the daughter of another member of the group. Inês visits Margaret in Foz. Later, Joaquim decides to use his right of reply: by law, the newspaper must publish his answer.

"The journalist rang me on the twenty-second," said Margaret. "He asked me whether my father had believed that the printer betrayed him. I said, 'My father believed it until the day he died. But I no longer do, and I have good reasons.' He thanked me very politely." She picked up a printout of the article and let it fall. "They used the first sentence. Not the second. Every word they printed is true, and the whole thing is a lie."
"Did you ask them to correct it?"

"Three times. The editor replied that they had reported my words accurately. Which they had." Margaret sat down. "I spent forty years translating other people's words, Inês. I know better than anyone that you can betray someone without changing a single word. All you have to do is choose which ones to keep."

"I took it to a conservation laboratory at the university in Lisbon, the week after the post appeared. Ink that has faded can sometimes be seen again under infrared light. It's an old technique; it was used long before anyone had heard of artificial intelligence. They sent me this yesterday."
The photograph showed the same page, but darker, strange, like an X-ray. And across it, perfectly legible, in Edward Hale's elegant handwriting:
They told me that J. gave them our names. I cannot believe it. I will not believe it until I hear it from him, and they will not let me see him. They say I must leave by Thursday.
Inês read it twice. "I cannot believe it," she said. "Not 'I cannot forgive him'."

"He didn't believe it." Margaret's voice was very low. "Not in 1973. It took him seventeen years of silence in a small town in Surrey to start believing it. Had he been able to speak to your grandfather even once, it would never have happened. But nobody was allowed to speak to anybody. That was the whole point."

That evening Inês sat with her grandfather at the kitchen table, as they had sat over her homework for years, but this time she held the pen. He dictated in Portuguese and she wrote, and every so often he stopped and asked her to read a sentence back, and changed one word, the way a printer corrects a proof. It was not an angry letter. It was very short. It said that he had been arrested on the sixteenth of March 1973, that he had spent nine days without sleep and thirteen months in prison, that he had never given any names, and that he had requested his file from the national archive so that anyone who wished could read the truth in the police's own words. It ended: I was not given a carnation. I walked past them. I did not think I deserved one, because I had lost a friend. I am beginning to think that the friend was lost to me by the same people who arrested me.

text: In the national archive, Joaquim, Margaret, Inês and Daniel are reading Joaquim's police file. As the "source of information", it names Margaret's father, Edward Hale. Next comes Edward's letter to a London friend, joking that Joaquim "saw spies everywhere".

Behind the summary was a photograph of a letter, slightly blurred, with a rubber stamp across the top: CORRESPONDÊNCIA INTERCEPTADA. Intercepted correspondence. It was addressed to a Mr Arthur Penrose, a publisher in London, and dated the second of February, 1973. The handwriting was the same elegant hand as on the water-stained page.

"He wrote it the same week," her grandfather said. His voice was steady. "The same week I typed that message in the Dickens. Alguém de dentro lê as nossas cartas. I meant inside the post office. My cousin worked at the sorting office, and he told me that some envelopes were arriving resealed, with the glue still wet. I tried to warn everyone the only way I could." He shook his head slowly. "And Edward thought I was being dramatic, and sat down and wrote to London to say so. And they read it."

There were the interrogation notes. For nine days, it was recorded, the prisoner had refused to answer any questions. On the ninth day an officer had written in the margin that the prisoner "shows no signs of cooperating" and recommended that "he be shown the Englishman's letter, in order to convince him that he has been betrayed". The next entry stated only that the letter had been shown to the prisoner and that he had "remained silent".

There was another note, written in the first days after the arrests, about "the British subject". It was recommended that he should not be arrested, since this "would cause problems with the British consulate and the foreign press". Instead, it was suggested that he be informed that "the printer has confessed", so that he would leave the country quickly and quietly. In the margin, someone had written: Done. He believed it.

It was dated the twenty-first of March, 1973, the day before Edward Hale left Portugal. It was written in formal Portuguese, with two small grammatical mistakes that Margaret would correct in her head for the rest of her life. It was addressed to the director of the political police. In it, Edward Hale stated that he alone had organised the group, that he alone had chosen and translated the texts, and that the printer Joaquim Carvalho had only printed what he had been paid to print, without understanding its content. He offered to sign a full confession, and to remain in Portugal and be tried, on one condition: that Joaquim Carvalho and the three students be released.

"'It is a far, far better thing that I do,'" he was saying, very softly, in English. "The fool. The sentimental fool. He would have gone to prison for me. And he would have cried at the end of it." He laughed, and his eyes were wet. "He was careless, Margaret. Your father was careless, and brave, and he wrote too many letters. But he was never a traitor."
"Neither were you," said Margaret, through her fingers. "Neither were you. And they made sure that each of you spent the rest of your life believing the other one was."

writing.task: Exam practice. "Does a society have a duty to remember its past, even when the past is painful?" Write an **opinion essay** (150 to 180 words). Present your point of view clearly, give reasons and examples, and write a conclusion.
writing.model: Some people believe that painful periods of history should be left behind, so that a country can move on. I disagree. In my view, a democratic society has a duty to remember its past, especially when that past is painful. First of all, memory protects the present. Portugal lived under a dictatorship for almost fifty years, with censorship, political prisoners and a secret police. If young people do not know this, they may not understand why freedom of expression and free elections matter, or how easily they can be lost. Secondly, remembering is a way of doing justice to the victims. Many people who were arrested or tortured never received an apology, and the least we can do is to know their stories. Of course, memory must be honest. Remembering is not the same as seeking revenge, and history should be studied with documents and evidence, not with rumours or invented stories. To conclude, a society that forgets its past is like a person without a memory: easy to deceive and likely to repeat the same mistakes.
