Past Continuouswas/were workingwhile, as, at 8 o'clock yesterday
Present Perfecthave/has workedfor, since, ever, never, just, already, yet, so far
Present Perfect Cont.have/has been workingfor, since, all day, how long, lately
Past Perfecthad workedby the time, before, after, already, when
Past Perfect Cont.had been workingfor, since (before a past moment)
Future (will / going to)will work / am going to worktomorrow, next…, soon, I think · plans, evidence
Future Perfect (Cont.)will have (been) work(ed/ing)by then, by 2030, by the time, for … by
Rephrasing tip: read the time markers first; keep the meaning, change the structure. I started here in 2020. → I have been working here since 2020. · It's a long time since we met. → We haven't met for a long time.

sebenta.title: Inversion
sebenta.html:
Inversion = putting the auxiliary before the subject (as in a question) for emphasis or a formal, literary tone. If there is no auxiliary, use do / does / did. I have never seen such chaos. → Never have I seen such chaos. · She rarely complains. → Rarely does she complain.

After negative and restrictive adverbials (at the start of the sentence)

ExpressionExample
Never / Rarely / Seldom / LittleNever had I felt so alone. · Seldom do we get a second chance. · Little did they know what was coming.
Not only … but (also)Not only did he lie, but he also blamed us.
No sooner … than
Hardly / Scarcely / Barely … when (past perfect)		No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang.
Hardly had I arrived when it started to rain.
Only + time / condition: only then, only after, only when, only if, only by -ing, only later (inversion in the main clause)Only when she left did I realise my mistake.
Only by working hard can you succeed.
Not until + clause / nounNot until the next day did we hear the news.
Under no circumstances / On no account / In no way / At no time / NowhereUnder no circumstances should you open this door. · Nowhere is this clearer than in cities.
Neither / Nor / So (agreement)I don't drive, and neither does my brother. · She passed, and so did I.

So · such · conditionals · place

StructureExample
So + adjective / adverb + auxiliary + subject + thatSo loud was the music that the neighbours complained.
Such + be + noun phrase + thatSuch was the demand that tickets sold out in minutes.
Conditional without if: Had (3rd) · Were (2nd) · Should (1st, formal)Had I known, I would have helped. · Were I in your position, I'd refuse. · Should you need anything, call reception. (negative: Had it not been for…)
Place / movement adverbials (full verb before subject, literary)Here comes the bus. · On the hill stood a castle. · Out ran the dog. (no inversion with pronouns: Here it comes)
After as / than (formal comparisons)She was anxious, as were her parents. · He earns more than does his boss.
Watch out: inversion only in the clause introduced by the adverbial: Not until he apologised did she forgive him (not did he apologise). No inversion when the negative word is not at the start: I have never seen it. Do not add do when there is already an auxiliary: Rarely has he been (not rarely does he has been).

sebenta.title: Cleft sentences
sebenta.html:
A cleft ("split") sentence divides one message into two clauses to highlight one element: the person, thing, time, place or reason. Neutral: Ana broke the vase yesterday.

It-clefts: It + be + highlighted element + that / who

Highlighting…Example
the subject (person)It was Ana who / that broke the vase.
the object (thing)It was the vase that Ana broke (not the plate).
time / place / mannerIt was yesterday that she broke it. · It was in the kitchen that it happened. · It was by accident that she did it.
negative / contrastIt wasn't the money that mattered, but the principle. · It isn't until you lose something that you value it.

The verb be agrees with the tense of the original sentence (It was… / It is…). After a pronoun, use the object form: It was me who called (formal: It was I who called).

Wh-clefts: What / All / The reason… + clause + be + highlighted element

StructureExample
What + clause + is / was + noun / -ing / to-infinitiveWhat I need is a holiday. · What she did was (to) call the police. · What annoys me is his attitude.
All (that) + clause + is / was (= the only thing)All I want is some peace. · All you have to do is (to) sign here.
The reason (why) + clause + is / was + that / becauseThe reason why I left was that I was bored.
The person who / The thing that / The place where / The time whenThe person who helped me most was my aunt. · The place where we met was Porto.
Reversed wh-cleft (highlighted element first)A holiday is what I need. · Porto is where we met.
What happens / happened is / was (that) (narrative)What happened was that the car broke down.
Verb agreement: the verb after a what-clause is normally singular (What I like is the colours), though plural is possible with a plural noun (What I like are the colours). When the what-clause contains do, the second part can be a bare infinitive: What he did was apologise.
Typical rephrasing: "I only need one thing: time." → All I need is time. · "She chose the red one, not the blue one." → It was the red one that she chose. · "I admire her honesty." → What I admire is her honesty. · "He left because he was bored." → The reason why he left was that he was bored.

sebenta.title: Participle clauses
sebenta.html:
Participle clauses replace a full clause with a participle and make writing more concise and formal. The participle normally has the same subject as the main clause.

ParticipleMeaningExamples
Present (-ing)
active, same time or cause		= while / as / because + subject + verbFeeling tired, I went to bed early. (= Because I felt…)
Walking home, I saw an accident. (= While I was walking…)
Past (-ed / 3rd column)
passive meaning		= because / when + subject + be + p.p.Built in 1890, the bridge is now a museum. (= It was built…)
Left alone, the dog began to howl.
Perfect (having + p.p.)
earlier action		= after / because + subject + past perfectHaving finished the exam, we went out. (= After we had finished…)
Having been warned, he was careful.
Negativenot before the participleNot knowing the answer, I guessed. · Not having slept, she was irritable.

After conjunctions and prepositions

WordExample
when / while / before / after / since / until / once + -ing (or p.p.)Before leaving, lock the door. · When asked, he said nothing. · Once completed, the form must be signed.
on / upon + -ing (= as soon as) · by + -ing (method) · without + -ing · despite / in spite of + -ing · instead of + -ingOn hearing the news, she fainted. · He passed by studying hard. · She left without saying goodbye. · Despite being ill, he came.

Reduced relative clauses

Full relative clauseReduced (defining or non-defining)
The woman who is talking to Rui is my boss.The woman talking to Rui is my boss. (active → -ing)
The students who were selected will travel.The students selected will travel. (passive → p.p.)
The hotel, which was built in 1920, is listed.The hotel, built in 1920, is listed.

Only the relative pronoun as subject can be reduced: the book that I bought cannot become the book buying.

Dangling participles: the subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause. Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful (the trees were not walking) → Walking down the street, I thought the trees looked beautiful. A different subject can be stated (absolute clause, formal): The weather being awful, we stayed in. · Weather permitting, we'll sail.
Other uses: after verbs of perception (I saw him leaving / I heard my name called); result (The storm hit the coast, causing floods); spend / waste time + -ing; get / have something done (see p. 8).

sebenta.title: Advanced conditionals
sebenta.html:
TypeFormExample · use
Zeroif + present, presentIf you heat ice, it melts. (facts; if = when)
Firstif + present, will / can / may / imperativeIf it rains, we'll cancel. (real, future)
Secondif + past, would / could / mightIf I were you, I'd apologise. (unreal present / future, advice)
Thirdif + past perfect, would / could / might have + p.p.If you had told me, I could have helped. (unreal past, regret)
Mixedif + past perfect, would + verb
if + past, would have + p.p.		If I had taken the job, I'd be in Berlin now. (past → present)
If she weren't so stubborn, she'd have listened. (present → past)

Alternatives to if and special cases

ExpressionExample
unless (= if … not)I won't go unless you come. (= if you don't come)
provided / providing (that), as long as, on condition that (= only if)You can borrow it as long as you return it today.
in case (precaution; present or past, not will)Take an umbrella in case it rains. (≠ if it rains)
suppose / supposing, what if · even if · otherwise (= if not)Supposing you won, what would you do? · Hurry up, otherwise we'll miss the train.
but for / if it weren't for / if it hadn't been for / without + nounBut for your help, I would have failed. · If it weren't for the noise, I'd love this flat.
if + will / would (willingness, insistence, polite request)If you will keep interrupting, we'll never finish. · If you would wait here, sir.
if + should / happen to (less likely; formal) · inversion (p. 4)If you should / happen to see him, say hello. → Should you see him… · Had we left earlier, …

Wishes, regrets and preferences

StructureExample
wish / if only + past simple (present situation)I wish I knew the answer. · If only I were taller.
wish / if only + past perfect (past regret)I wish I hadn't said that.
wish / if only + would (annoyance, change)I wish you would stop complaining.
would rather / sooner + bare inf. · + subject + pastI'd rather stay. · I'd rather you didn't smoke here.
it's (high / about) time + subject + past · as if / as though + past (unreal)It's high time you found a job. · He acts as if he owned the place.

sebenta.title: Reported speech and passive review
sebenta.html:
Reported speech: the backshift

DirectReported
present simple / continuouspast simple / continuous
past simple / present perfectpast perfect
past perfect · would, could, might, should, ought tono change
will / can / may / mustwould / could / might / must or had to
DirectReported
now · today · tonightthen · that day · that night
yesterday · agothe day before · before
tomorrow · next weekthe next / following day · week
this · here · comethat · there · go
  • Questions: wh-word or if / whether + subject + verb, no do, no question mark. "Where were you?" → She asked (me) where I had been. · "Can you swim?" → He asked whether I could swim.
  • Commands and requests: tell / order / ask / warn + object + (not) to + infinitive. "Don't touch it!" → She told me not to touch it.
  • No backshift with a present reporting verb or a fact still true: He says he's busy. · She said water boils at 100 °C.
Reporting verb patternVerbsExample
verb + to-infinitiveagree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten, claim, demandHe refused to pay.
verb + object + to-infinitiveadvise, beg, encourage, invite, order, persuade, remind, urge, warnShe urged us to vote.
verb + -ing / + preposition + -ingadmit, deny, suggest, recommend · apologise for, accuse sb of, insist on, blame sb for, congratulate sb onHe admitted taking it. · They accused him of lying.

The passive: be (any tense) + past participle

TenseActivePassive
Present / past simpleThey recycle / recycled the waste.The waste is / was recycled.
Present / past continuousThey are / were recycling it.It is / was being recycled.
Present / past perfectThey have / had recycled it.It has / had been recycled.
Future · going to · modalsThey will / are going to / must recycle it.It will be / is going to be / must be recycled.
Perfect modals · infinitive · -ingThey should have recycled it. · I want them to recycle it.It should have been recycled. · I want it to be recycled. · I hate being watched.
  • Two objects → the person is usually the subject: They offered her a job. → She was offered a job. Verbs with prepositions keep them: The matter will be dealt with. Get + p.p. is informal: He got sacked.
  • Impersonal passive (say, think, believe, know, report, expect, consider, claim): It is said that he is rich. → He is said to be rich. · It was reported that he had left. → He was reported to have left.
  • Causative: have / get + object + p.p. (a service, or something unpleasant): We had the roof repaired. · She got her bag stolen. have sb do / get sb to do = make / persuade: I'll have him call you. · I got her to agree.

sebenta.title: Modal verbs review
sebenta.html:
Modals (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would) + bare infinitive; no -s, no do. Past or unreal meaning → modal + have + past participle. Semi-modals: have to, need to, be able to, ought to, be allowed to, had better, be supposed to.

FunctionPresent / futurePast
Abilitycan, be able to I can't swim.could (general) · was able to / managed to (one occasion) We managed to escape. · could have + p.p. (ability not used) I could have won.
Permissioncan / could / may (formal), be allowed to May I leave?could, was allowed to We were allowed to stay up.
Prohibitionmustn't, can't, may not, be not allowed to You mustn't park here.couldn't, wasn't allowed to
Obligationmust (speaker) · have to (external) · should / ought to / be supposed to (weaker) I must finish. · I have to wear a tie.had to We had to queue. · was supposed to (but didn't) You were supposed to call me.
No obligationdon't have to, don't need to, needn't You needn't come.didn't have to / didn't need to (not necessary, probably not done) · needn't have + p.p. (done, but unnecessary) You needn't have cooked – we'd eaten.
Adviceshould / ought to · had better (not) (warning) You'd better leave now.should have / ought to have + p.p. (criticism, regret) You should have asked. · shouldn't have + p.p.
Deduction: certainmust + verb / be + -ing He must be joking.must have + p.p. They must have left.
Deduction: possiblemay / might / could (+ well) She might be asleep.may / might / could have + p.p. He may have missed the bus. · might have (reproach) You might have told me!
Deduction: impossiblecan't / couldn't That can't be true.can't / couldn't have + p.p. He can't have forgotten.
Requests, offerscan / could / would you…? · shall I…? · would you mind + -ing?—
Habitwill (typical behaviour) He'll sit there for hours.would / used to We would walk to school.
Expectationshould / ought to The parcel should arrive today.should have + p.p. (expected but didn't) It should have arrived by now.
Three classic traps: mustn't (forbidden) ≠ don't have to (not necessary) · didn't need to (unnecessary, so I didn't) ≠ needn't have (I did it, but it was unnecessary) · could (general past ability) ≠ was able to / managed to (succeeded once). Also: after must, can't, may for deduction about the present use be + -ing for actions: She must be working late.
Rephrasing bank: It's possible that he left. → He may have left. · It wasn't necessary to book. → You didn't need to book. · I'm sure she didn't see us. → She can't have seen us. · It was a mistake to leave. → We shouldn't have left. · Perhaps they're abroad. → They might be abroad. · Smoking is forbidden. → You mustn't / aren't allowed to smoke.

sebenta.title: Connectors
sebenta.html:
FunctionConnectors (F = formal · I = informal / neutral)Examples
Contrastbut, yet (between clauses) · although / though / even though + clause · despite / in spite of + noun / -ing / the fact that · however, nevertheless, nonetheless (F) · on the other hand, in contrast, conversely · whereas / while (comparison)Although it's cheap, it's reliable. · Despite the cost, … · It's cheap. However, it breaks easily. · Rural areas are quiet, whereas cities are noisy.
Concessionadmittedly, granted, it is true that … but · even so, all the same, stillAdmittedly, it is expensive; even so, it is worth it.
Resultso (I) · therefore, thus, hence, consequently, as a result, accordingly (F) · so … that / such … thatDemand fell. Consequently, prices dropped. · It was so cold that the river froze.
Reasonbecause, as, since + clause · because of, due to, owing to, on account of + noun · for (F, literary)The match was cancelled owing to the storm. · Since you ask, I'll explain.
Purposeto / in order (not) to / so as (not) to + inf. · so that + can / will / could / would · with a view to / with the aim of + -ing (F)We left early so as not to miss it. · Save now so that you can travel later.
Additionand, also, too, as well · both … and, not only … but also · moreover, furthermore, in addition, what is more, besides (F) · apart from / in addition to + nounThe scheme is costly. Furthermore, it is unpopular. · Apart from the price, I like it.
Sequencefirst(ly), to begin with, secondly, then, next, subsequently, afterwards, meanwhile, finally, lastly, eventuallyTo begin with, … Subsequently, … Lastly, …
Examplefor example / for instance, such as, like (I), namely, in particular, notably, to illustrateSome countries, notably Norway, tax cars heavily.
Clarifying · emphasisin other words, that is (to say), i.e. · indeed, in fact, above all, undoubtedlyIn other words, the plan failed. · It is cheap; indeed, the cheapest.
Opinionin my opinion / view, to my mind, personally, as far as I am concerned, I firmly believe, it seems to meTo my mind, the benefits outweigh the risks.
Conclusionin conclusion, to sum up, to conclude, all in all, on the whole, overall, taking everything into account, on balanceOn balance, the policy has been a success.
Punctuation and register: however, therefore, moreover… start a new sentence and take a comma (…; however, … / … . However, …), never , however joining two clauses. Despite / in spite of + noun (despite of); although + clause (although of). Avoid and, but, so at the start of formal sentences; prefer moreover, however, therefore. Do not stack connectors: one per idea.
Argumentative essay (opinion / for-and-against): ① Introduction: context + thesis (It is often argued that… This essay will…) ② Paragraph 2: first argument + example (Firstly, … For instance, …) ③ Paragraph 3: second argument or counter-argument (On the other hand, … Nevertheless, …) ④ Conclusion: restate position (To sum up, … In my view, …). One idea per paragraph; topic sentence first.

sebenta.html:
Register = adapting language to the reader and purpose. Application letters, reports, complaints and essays are formal; an email to a friend, a blog post or a story is informal / neutral. Be consistent from the first line to the last.

Exam writing bank

Text typeStructure · key language
Argumentative essayIntro (context + thesis) → arguments with examples → counter-argument → conclusion. It is widely believed that… · There are several reasons why… · One major advantage is… · Critics argue that…, however… · Taking everything into account, …
Letter / email of applicationDear Sir or Madam, → reason for writing + where you saw the job → qualifications and experience → personal qualities → availability + CV attached → I look forward to hearing from you. → Yours faithfully, + full name.
Formal letter of complaintI am writing to express my dissatisfaction with… · On (date) I purchased… · Unfortunately, … · I would therefore be grateful if you could refund / replace… · I expect a prompt reply. · Yours faithfully / sincerely,
ArticleCatchy title + rhetorical question or anecdote to open → paragraphs with subheadings → direct address to the reader (Have you ever…? Imagine…) → memorable final line. Neutral / semi-formal, lively.
ReportTitle + To / From / Date / Subject → headings: Introduction (aim) · Findings · Recommendations · Conclusion → impersonal, passive, bullet points allowed. The aim of this report is to… · It was found that… · It is recommended that…
ReviewTitle + what (film / book / app) → brief summary (no spoilers, present tense) → strengths and weaknesses → recommendation. Set in… · The plot revolves around… · The acting is superb / wooden. · Well worth seeing / I would not recommend it to…
Punctuation reminder: capitals for days, months, nationalities and languages; a comma after a connector at the start of a sentence (However, …) and after a first if-clause; no comma before that; commas around non-defining relative clauses; apostrophes for possession and contractions, never for plurals.
